items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Following discussions in the
Business Committee, I seek leave for there to be no general debate on 11 December
2013. I understand that later that day there wi ll be an adjournment debate, in which
members should be able to traverse most of  the matters that might be covered in a
general debate.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
There appears to be none.
Government—Relationship with Support Partners
1. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister:
Does he have confidence in the stability of his Government?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Will he depend on Mr Banks’ vote to pass legislation for the
remainder of this term?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That will depend, obviously, on  whether it is either a
confidence and supply issue or case by case, as we deal with every party in Parliament.
But, in principle, yes, where Mr Banks choos es to exercise that vote on behalf of the
ACT Party.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: If it is on a case by case basis, as the Prime Minister has said,
what does it say that he could not muster a majority for his copper tax or the Resource
Management Act changes, and how can the co untry be confident of stable Government
over the next year?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The fact that we have not introduced the Resource
Management Act legislation does not m ean that we cannot actually command a
majority. The member might actu ally be quite surprised by th at, but we will leave that,
actually, for another day. In terms of the c opper tax, that was never actually tested. We
were aware that our partners would not vot e for it and we decided not to introduce it.
But, anyway, we would not have done so, be cause after that poin t the retail service
providers decided that they did not want to  do a deal with Chorus, so it was a moot
point.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does the Prime Minister now know for certain that the Hon
Peter Dunne did not leak the Kitteridge report?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I do not know the answer to that. I do not believe that was
the purpose of the privileges claim.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Then how could he accept him back in his Cabinet?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because, firstly, we have not done that and, secondly, we
accept the member at his word.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does he agree with Colin Cr aig that man may never have
walked on the moon?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Rt Hon Prime Minister, as far as he has responsibility.
15198 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Dec 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and one of the great privileg es of being Prime Minister is
that you get the opportunity firsthand to ha ve some unique experiences. One of mine
was having—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: You’ve been on the moon?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I have not been to the m oon. I have not been to the moon,
although I know that Labour’s economic polic ies are developed up there. But, no. As
Prime Minister, I had dinner with Buzz Aldrin  one night. Buzz looked pretty convinced
that he had been to the moon, and he would know.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Will one of his unique experiences be to have Colin Craig land
on “Planet Key”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, there are a lot of people who would like to be part of
“Planet Key”, as we saw in the last el ection, when over a million people voted for
National. And how many voted for Labour? Was it 300,000 or 400,000?

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Not any more, Johnny.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, actually, our polling last night did not indicate that.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Which is worse: propping up a dying Government based on the
vote of a potential electoral fraudster—an  ex-Minister whom he thinks may have
released secret documents—or an extremist who put out 20,000 leaflets saying that John
Key should not be the Prime Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We deal with MMP. That requires any political party or group
of parties to get 61 votes. Come the next election, it will be the same situation. It will be
no different for the Labour Pa rty than it will be for the National Party. But what I can
say, based on all the things I see, is that the probability of Nati onal being able to get
those 61 seats is far greate r than it is for Labour. The one difference, though, between
election 2014 and election 2011 is that I will go into election 2014 with 100 percent of
my caucus wanting me to get there and you, Mr  Cunliffe, will go th ere with less than a
third of your caucus wanting you to get there.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: In the run-up to this election, does the Prime Minister continue
to intend to hop from cloud to cloud; if so, under which cloud will he find the Hon John
Banks and on which cloud will he find Colin Craig?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not know, but I will find the Labour Party’s economic
policies in cloud-cuckoo-land.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does the Prime Minister’s statement that he has to take Mr
Dunne at his word in respect of his denial m ean that he believes Mr Dunne did not leak
the Kitteridge report?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member has, on numerous occasions, strongly said that he
did not leak the report. I accept the member at his word. There was no conclusion to that
report.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How legitimate does he believe his asset sales programme is,
given that it was passed by a single vote in this House and th at that single vote was the
vote of John Banks, the discre dited MP who is currently in  front of the courts for
electoral fraud?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, firstly, I think it is re ally important that we recognise
and actually respect that every New Zealander is innocent unless they are proven guilty.
We, as members of this House, actually ha ve a responsibility, I believe, to at least
accept that basic principle, which we expect  other New Zealanders to accept. Secondly,
in a parliamentary majority in this Parl iament, you are required to get 61 votes, and
those 61 legitimate votes are required. We have them; that is called a majority. If Russel
Norman is telling us that if one day—goodness knows if it ever happens—he is part of a
Government, he would not count that as a majority, that is a really interesting
proposition, which he should get to his feet  and tell New Zeala nders about now. The
4 Dec 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 15199
truth is that it is just typical Russel  Norman—says one thing, will do something
completely different. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! And that includes the member.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: My question to the Prime Minister is in relation to his previous
answer. Given that the courts have found that John Banks took a $15,000 donation
from—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The difficulty I am anticipat ing with this question is that
there is a case now that is sub judice—before the court. I am certainly not ruling that
question out of order, but I am going to ask the member to rephrase it in such a way that
he does not breach Standing Order 112 by referri ng to a case that is now potentially sub
judice.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I was actually quoting from
the judge’s decision in the most recent judici al review that Mr Banks went to court
about—exactly that case.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No. Speaking to the point—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear from the Hon Gerry Brownlee.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I think that is a very reckless comment for Dr Norman to
have made. There has been no finding; there has been simply a determination that it
should proceed to a trial—quite  a different matter. Dr Norman has, I think, got himself
in some trouble by implying that there has been a judgment, when there has not been.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear from the Rt Hon Winston Peters.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: With respect, the sub judice rule here involves whether or
not Mr Banks knowingly had a declaration filled out, and that is the matter that is before
the court. It is not whether he received  the money. That has been accepted by his
lawyer, and it was by him at court. The sub judice rule concerns his knowledge as to
that declaration of return. That is a differe nt matter, and Dr Norman has not traversed
that at all.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Let me hear again from the member , but I would just ask him to be
careful and consistent with the Standing Orde rs and Speakers’ rulings on this matter,
which is quite complicated and difficult.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that John Banks received a $15,000 donation from
Skycity, does he believe that  it is legitimate for him to rely on John Banks’ vote in
giving Skycity concessions to massively expand its operations?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. Is that not going right to
the heart of the case that is going to the court?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No, it’s not.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No, well, I am sorry. There are constitutional experts and
lawyers over here who might think so, but—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The member will resume his seat. I
accept that this is a very difficult issue, but I think the way that question is now worded
is in order, and it is stating facts that ar e now in the public arena. The Prime Minister
can answer that question.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The issue, though, is
how any donation was received, and for him to assert it was received by Mr Banks is, at
this point, wrong.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: But that was not the question that—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: It was. He said: “Given that he received …”. Those words
are wrong.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The issue is how it was th en described—the receipt of it.
That is the issue. I do not think there is mu ch doubt, to the best of my knowledge, that
15200 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Dec 2013
the donation was received. It is then a matter of how it was returne d. I have ruled that
the Prime Minister can answer the question, and that is the absolute end of the matter.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not accept the premise of the question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he believe that it does damage to the reputation of this
House that the vote on the Skycity bill, whic h gave enormous concessions to Skycity,
was reliant on the vote of John Banks, w ho received a $15,000 donation from Skycity
and is currently before the courts on exactly that issue?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Once again, the member has proved that he cannot count. The
majority was two, not one.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Did he or any of his advisers or colleagues pressure John Banks
to stay on as an MP, despite the fact that he  faces a trial for electoral fraud, because his
Government relies on the single vote provided by that MP in this House to pass his most
unpopular legislation like asset sales?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, not to the best of my knowledge.
Economy—Export Sector Performance, Government Financial Position, and
Growth
2. KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What
reports has he received on progress in lifting New Zealand’s export performance and
reducing its reliance on borrowing from overseas lenders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have received a number of reports
confirming strong performance by New Zealand’s exporters, particularly in those areas
where the Opposition was most concerned—that is, in the regions and in manufacturing.
Exporters have performed well despite str ong headwinds from a high Kiwi dollar and
difficult export conditions in our traditional markets. Our terms of trade rose 7.5 percent
in the September quarter due to export prices rising faster than import prices. This is the
highest terms of trade level since 1973, as determined by prices for our exports in world
markets. The trade deficit for October was $168 million, the lowest for any October
month since the mid-1990s. So prices in world markets are higher than we expected, but
our exporters are performing better than was expected.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: What progress is the Gove rnment making in reducing
New Zealand’s external vulnerabilities, part icularly in bringing down the longstanding
current account deficit?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: First of all, the Government cannot have a direct effect on
the current account deficit. What we can do is try to create conditions where our
exporters thrive and where imported inflation is relatively low. Last week Statistics
New Zealand issued the national accounts for the March 2013 year. They included
significant upwards revisions to the estimates of spending by overseas visitors. This has
had the effect of boosting our service e xports and decreasing the amount that was
originally attributed to the private consumption of households. As a result, our recorded
level of household and nati onal saving has increased, wh ereas the current account
deficit for the year to March 2013 has decr eased. It was estimated previously at 4.5
percent of GDP, and it has now  been re-estimated at 3.9 percent of GDP. So the
statisticians have discovered that we ar e doing more exporting and less consuming than
they thought.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: What steps has the Government taken to help to rebalance
the economy towards more savings and expo rts and to veer away from excessive
consumption, borrowing, and Government spending, which marked the mid-2000s?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There is certainly more to do to rebalance this economy. It
has been difficult to have the amount of e xport growth we would like to see when the
exchange rate has been so high. And it has been a wee bit difficult to reduce
Government spending when we have had th e earthquakes in Christ church requiring us
4 Dec 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 15201
to commit up to $15 billion to rebuild Chri stchurch. But despite those headwinds we
implemented a tax package in 2010 that favoured savings and exports over consumption
and property speculation. The Business Growth  Agenda supports businesses to invest
and employ, and, as a result, the tradable sector, which was in recession for several
years up to 2008, has grown by 11.6 percent fro m its trough in the second quarter of
2009. But there is still much more work to do.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: What economic approaches would halt the progress being
made in supporting exports, productivity, investment, and jobs?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We have a reasonably good idea what would have a negative
effect on New Zealand’s now positive growth prospects, and those are the things that
affected our growth prospects badly in th e mid-2000s. Three factors were pretty clear
from that: an excessive rise in house pri ces, which doubled in a bout 10 years; runaway
Government spending, particularly from 2005 onwards; and regulatory change that
inhibited business and export investment and savings. They  were the policies of the
Labour Party. We want to avoid those traps this time around.
Student Achievement—OECD Report and Impact of Government Strategies
3. HONE HARAWIRA (Leader—Mana)  to the Minister of Education : What
responsibility does she accept for the New Zealand results as identified in the OECD’s
PISA report released yesterday, which show s New Zealand’s test scores in maths,
reading and science have all deteriorated  under her watch, and that New Zealand’s
education system has failed to keep pace with the educational achievements of other
countries, also under her watch?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I am the
Minister of Education, and these responsibilities fall to me. These results are serious but
not surprising. The Government is serious ab out the plan we have for fixing this. The
group of 15-year-olds who were assessed last y ear has been in the system for about 11
years, since 2001-02. Playing the blame game does not help them. These students were
not caught by national standard s, but they will be caught  by National Certificate of
Educational Achievement level 2 and the Y outh Guarantee, where the Government has
ambitious targets to make sure our children and young people are succeeding.

items.speaker: Hone Harawira
items.text: What responsibility does the Minist er accept for the fact that the
OECD recommendation talked about equity , increasing resources, and targeting
disadvantaged children through additional econo mic assistance, including free meals in
schools for students from poor fa milies, yet her Government ha s chosen to ignore all of
that and focus on everything else, including national standards, private education,
charter schools, cuts for science advisers , attacks on the unions, criticising teacher
standards and then paying them through a broken system called Novopay, the sum
result of which has been to confuse, confound, and demoralise—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That question now is sufficiently long enough.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Our Government is this year  investing $9.7 billion into
Vote Education—the highest it has ever b een. That is a 74 percent increase on early
childhood education and a 40 percent increas e on schooling. We have invested $37.5
million this year in raising the quality of teaching so that, all across the system, every
child will get a better education. We are investing in a data-rich  environment because
we do not want to guess; we want to know specifically who and where we need to be
helping, and for what. So last week we announced $10.5 million into maths and science
resources, and we announced $31.5 million to  invest into Building on Success, which
are the best elements of Te P ūtahitanga M ātauranga, He K ākano, Starpath, and
Gateway, all of which have been proven to be successful for M āori and Pasifika. In
terms of—
15202 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Dec 2013

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is now a very long answer to a very long question.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What do the Programme for International Student Assessment
2012 results tell us about the achievement of New Zealand’s young people?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: The results from the Program me for International Student
Assessment 2012 confirm what we know about student achievement in New Zealand.
Our highest-achieving students are comparable with the best in the world. However, the
whole education system needs to be better geared to support all of our students to
succeed. We continue to work to ensure we have a well-performing system, but it is not
performing for all. That is why we are focu sed on raising achievement for five out of
five learners.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Tēnā koutou e te Whare. How is it not
a failure after 5 years of her Government that New Zealand is one of the only countries
in the developed world where the chances of poor kids doing well at school has actually
decreased in the years that National has been in power?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: What the Programme for International Student Assessment
results tell us, for those who have actually an alysed them, is that of the factors that
contribute to failure, there is a correlation between underachievement and low socio-
economic status, and it amounts to 18 percent. Eighty-two percent rela tes to quality of
teaching and leadership, relates to turning up to school every day, and relates to turning
up on time. We are interested in all of thos e factors because it is a partnership between
schools and parents in the community that will  affect the results we want for all New
Zealanders.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: Why has equity in New Zeal and education deteriorated,
according to the Programme for Internationa l Student Assessment, since National came
to power, while Australia has managed to increase the chances of poorer kids doing well
there in exactly the same time period?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Rather than get into comparisons between those particular
systems—because actually that information is not accurate—what we have happening
here is that we now have nearly 96 percen t of all kids under 5 going to early childhood
education. This is a significant increase, and addresses equity issues.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. The Minister is giving a
great background on early childhood education, but the question was—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume her seat. The question was around
the difference of equity and performance in New Zealand and Australia. The Minister
addressed that straight away. She was sa ying that she did not agree with that
information.

items.speaker: Hone Harawira
items.text: What responsibility does the Minist er accept for saying that “New
Zealand has a good track-record on the international stage, ranking 7th in the world … in
reading …”, when just 4 months later, under her watch, we dropped to 13th in the world;
or does she instead hold to her ne w view that it is not that we  are doing so bad, it is just
that the Chinese are doing so much better?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: If the honourable member had used the full quote from me,
what I actually said was that under the prev ious Programme for International Student
Assessment results, New Zealand was se venth on that ranking for reading. But
disaggregated by ethnicity, M āori were 34 th, and Pasifika were 44 th. In every speech I
gave I pointed that out, and pointed out that the challenge to us was to get excellence in
the system for everyone.
State-owned Assets, Sales—Estimated Revenue, Genesis Energy, and Public
Support
4. Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance : Why has
he revised the estimated proceeds from asset sales down to a minimum of $4.6 billion?
4 Dec 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 15203

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In the first place, it is Treasury’s
estimate rather than the Government’s. As I said this morning, Treasury figures in the
Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update will revise the estimated range of proceeds to
$4.6 billion to $5 billion, with a mid-point of $4.8 billion. The revised assumption of the
share sale proceeds is based principally on th e fact that Solid Energy is clearly in no
position to be sold any time soon. The proceeds  will be less, mainly because one less
company will be sold. It also takes account of the results of the share offers to date and,
of course, these provide the onl y real market valuations that the energy companies have
ever had. Those values reflect the fact that  all electricity companies in New Zealand
have lost value, partly because of un certainty around the future price track for
electricity, and partly because of political uncertainty generated by alternative
regulatory proposals.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Why has he taken so long to revise the estimated proceeds
from asset sales, given that he told the public  as far back as August last year that Solid
Energy was not fit for sale and he has alrea dy come in more than $1 billion short on the
sales so far?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As I said, it is Treasury’s role to make the estimates, and it
has statutory requirements that have to be met for the degree of certainty about any
estimates it makes.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: How does he reconcile his statement to the Finance and
Expenditure Committee today that “The G overnment never said it was going to
maximise the value for taxpayers from the sales.” with his statement at the media stand-
up directly after his presenta tion at the Finance and Expendi ture Committee today that
“We have an obligation to protect the value of taxpayers’ investments.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Very easily. In the Finance and Expenditure Committee I
was asked about the conditions under which the Government made the sales, and I made
it clear, for instance, that the Government  decided it would reta in 51 percent of the
companies when, if it sold 100 percent of the companies, it would get more for them. In
the stand-up I was asked about KiwiRail in qu ite some detail. I made it clear that the
Government’s role in respect of KiwiRail is to protect the taxpayers ’ value, bearing in
mind that the reason we own these assets is  that hard-working Ne w Zealanders get to
the end of the week and very generously ha nd us 25 percent of their pay packet. They
could make good use of it. When we get it, just because it adds up to billions, it does not
mean we should be irresponsible. It means we should be very, very careful with the
$200 and $300 weekly payments that New Zealanders make to us.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: How can he claim the asset sales programme is a success
when he will not achieve the minimum $5 billion he promised after the forecasting by
his own Prime Minister in 2011 that $10 billion could be raised from this, plus he failed
to achieve widespread ownership and the pow er companies are today trading at record
lows?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Opposition cannot have it both ways. If it says that the
shares trading below their sale price is a failure, it certainly would say that if the shares
were trading above the sale value, then that was a failure. The Opposition cannot have it
both that we ripped off the inve stors and that we gave away the taxpayers’ assets. Both
of those things cannot be true. The sales were  a success. We gave out share certificates
to New Zealanders, and in return for th at we have $4 billion in the bank. I know it
worries the Opposition that we are going to be  spending that on public assets when it
cannot—because it would have to borrow that  money from foreign bankers, whom it
seems much more interested in—and when we want to provide investment opportunities
for New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Will the Government still proceed with the partial asset sale
of Genesis Energy on the current timetable; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, that is our intention. If the member means that the
referendum should determine that decision, I would put this proposition to him: if the
Opposition believes the referendum will show  overwhelming opposition to the sales,
then it should take it seriously and pr omise to buy the assets back. Everyone knows
what the Government will say. The quest ion is whether the Opposition takes the
referendum seriously. If Opposition members will not promise to buy the assets back,
then they are defying the will of the New Zealand public.
Science and Technology—Science and Society Project and Other Initiatives
5. SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki) to the Minister of Science and

items.speaker: Innovation
items.text: What steps is the Government ta king to improve the understanding, skills
and adoption of science and technology in New Zealand society?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government’s
view is that science is vital for New Zeal and’s future. We have, of course, increased
total funding for science, innovation, and research across the Government to $1.36
billion. Along the way, we have establ ished Callaghan Innovation, committed $278
million just this year for 51 new projects in science investment, and committed just
under half a billion dollars for 10 National Science Challenges. The National Science
Challenges panel recommended a further spec ial challenge to improve New Zealand’s
understanding and appreciation of science, and last week th e Minister of Education and
I announced the Science and Society project to  lift achievement in maths and science,
plus science literacy, across New Zealand.
Simon O’Connor : What steps is the Government  taking to lift achievement by
young people in maths and science?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: As the latest Programme for International Student
Assessment results demonstrate, it is critic al that we keep improving the understanding
of science and technology in this country, and improve young New Zealanders’ skills in
this area. New Zealand needs more young people with science, technology, engineering,
and maths skills in our workforce to help us be internationally competitive and to meet
our future labour market needs. As part of  the first phase of the Science and Society
project, last week Minister  Parata and I announced that the Government has committed
$10.5 million in additional funding for schools to raise student achievement in maths
and science. Also, more than half a million dollars is going into the development of
more than 60 science learning resources.
Simon O’Connor: What are the objectives of the Science and Society project?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Science and Society project is a unique venture
between the science sector and the education sector to lift achievement in science,
technology, engineering, and maths subjects, and also raise New Zealanders’ science
literacy more generally. [Interruption] Of course, there are some people we cannot help,
and they are on the other side of th e House. Aside from improving young New
Zealanders’ science skills, we also need to  improve science literacy right across the
population. A 2010 ACNielsen survey  showed that although public trust in science and
support for science funding is healthy, a lot of people have  a low appreciation of the
benefits of science, and the Science and So ciety project will coor dinate efforts across
Government to lift our literacy. The Prime Minister’s Chief Science Advisor, Sir Peter
Gluckman, will chair the reference group of experts to advise officials and Ministers.
4 Dec 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 15205
Health Targets—Progress
6. Dr PAUL HUTCHISON (National—Hunua)  to the Minister of Health : What
improvements in health services are shown in the latest health targets results?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The latest health targets results have
recently been published and they show con tinuing improvement, with record numbers
of patients benefiting from surgery and 91 pe rcent of 8-month-olds immunised. These
improvements in getting elective surgery mean that over the last 5 years on average
8,000 more patients a year have been treated.  These latest results also show that 93
percent of emergency department patients we re seen, treated, or discharged within 6
hours. This is the best wint er emergency department re sult since the targets began.
These better health services are the result of  the hard work of our health professionals,
helped by the average extra $500  million a year this Govern ment has invested into our
public health service.

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
items.text: What reports has he received on emergency department patients
benefiting from information technology advances?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: There are some exciting information technology advances that
are improving emergency department clinicians’ ability to provide better patient care. In
the Wairarapa District Health Board, the Waikato District Health Board, and the
Canterbury District Health Board, with the patient’s permission, emergency department
clinicians are able to access a summary of the patient’s primary-care information held
by their general practitioner. This includes the medicines they are on, their lab results,
and any other problems the patient may ha ve. This technology gives the emergency
department clinicians the opportunity to act  much more quickly, knowing they have up-
to-date data they can trust and, more importa nt, the patient does not have to tell their
story umpteen times to every clinician they meet.

items.text: In light of that answer, and if  there are such positive results by

Welfare Fraud—Information Sharing Between Agencies and Further Deterrents
7. Hon PHIL HEATLEY (National—Whangarei)  to the Associate Minister for

items.speaker: Social Development
items.text: How is the enhanced information sharing between the Ministry of
Social Development and Inland Revenue de livering on the Government’s promise to
crack down on welfare fraud?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.role: Associate Mi nister for Social Development
items.text: Our
enhanced information-sharing between the Inland Revenue Department and the
Ministry of Social Developmen t is working well. Since it be gan in March this year, the
ministry has identified and put a stop to mo re than 5,300 benefits that people were not
entitled to, and corrected another 3,000 who were not receiving correct support. Those
5,300 were costing the taxpayer a bare mini mum of $56 million per year. Although it is
great to see these people getting back into work, they should not have been taking
money they were no longer entitled to.
15206 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Dec 2013

items.speaker: Hon Phil Heatley
items.text: How does this enhanced information-sharing fit with other new
measures the Government has introduced to prevent, detect, and punish welfare fraud?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: The key aim of the packag e of reforms that this
Government introduced earlier this year is to  stop welfare fraud as soon as possible. I
am pleased with the results of our information sharing, as it is allowing us to catch fraud
we might otherwise have missed and stop ille gitimate benefits early, before the debt
really mounts up. This perfectly compleme nts other preventive measures such as
streamlined investigation processes, great er scrutiny of beneficiaries who have
previously ripped us off, and providing fo llow-up support to new sole parent support
beneficiaries.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Heatley
items.text: What is the intention behind trialling home visits to check in with
new beneficiaries receiving sole parent support?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: We recognise that for those receiving a benefit
dependent on their relationship status, navi gating the benefit rule s can be challenging.
Although most do it successfully those who do not end up taking money that they are
not entitled to and can be left with a massi ve debt and a fraud c onviction at the end of
the process. The intention behind trialling a number of methods of contact, including
offering to meet at their home, is to look at  the best way to keep in touch with sole
parent beneficiaries at a time when we know that their circumstances frequently change
at 14 weeks to 16 weeks after st arting to receive the benefit. There is no sinister intent.
This should be a check-in and not a checking-up.
Student Achievement—OECD Report and Impact of Government Strategies
8. CHRIS HIPKINS (Labour—Rimutaka)  to the Minister of Education : Is she
satisfied that the Government’s educational pr iorities are leading to  an improvement in
student achievement; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes, although we constantly
strive to do better. Why? Because the da ta speaks for itself: the highest-ever early
childhood education participation rate, at 95.8 percent; national standards show an
overall improvement, with nearly three-quarters of our students, on average, above or at
national standards; last year we had the highest-ever number of school leavers achieving
the National Certificate of Educational Ac hievement level 2, at 74 percent of school
leavers; and exemptions have fallen fr om over 4,000 under the Labour Government to
just 300 under this Government. Furthermore,  Andreas Schleicher, who is a special
adviser on education policy at the OECD and responsible for Programme for
International Student Assessment, noted in an email to me late last week that many of
the school policies that New Zealand is now pursuing are very much in line with the
conclusions in the OECD international report PISA 2012 Results: W hat Makes Schools
Successful?.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why did the Government cut funding for school science and

items.text: We have introduced a number of student achievement

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question asked—

items.text: Order! I do not need the question repeated. I am going to ask the

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why did the Government cut the funding for school science and
technology advisers, and does she now accept in light of our recent plunge on the
OECD rankings from 13th to 23rd in science that that was a mistake?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Because we decided to put that funding into student
achievement advisers who would work across the entire curriculum, including in maths,
science, and technology. We also decided that  we would target resources to those who
need it the most. We also decide d to invest in research that told us, for instance, that 40
percent of teachers do not feel confident to teach science and maths, so we are investing
to make sure that they do have that confidence and will raise their teaching practice.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why did the Government cut $35 million from teacher professional
development in its first Budget in 2009, and in light of her statement yesterday that New
Zealand’s decline in OECD rankings was pa rtly due to “under-investment in raising
teaching practice” will she now admit that that was a mistake as well?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Under this Government we ar e investing, on average, $70
million a year in professional learning and development—$70 million a year. We have
also taken heed of what the sector wanted, wh ich was to have more of it distributed out
in the regions. However, in listening to th e profession and hearing that it still does not
think that it is quite right,  I announced this week that we would review professional
learning and development, and are involving all of the organisations that have an
interest in it, because the profession, which we listened to, has asked for it.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: How does New Zealand compare with other countries
participating in the Programme for International Student Assessment?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: New Zealand remains above the OECD average. The
highest-achieving students in New Zealand are comparable with the best in the world. I
am sure all of us in this H ouse are pleased about that, but th ere is no doubt  that we are
now facing an achievement challenge. Fortun ately, this Government has been working
to a plan to address this. The other countries that we benchmark ourselves against,
Australia, Canada, Sweden, Finland, ha ve, to varying degrees, declined—[ Interruption]
I am sure that the Opposition members are interested, going by their response. Those
countries have declined while the performance of education systems in Asia—Shanghai,
China; Hong Kong, China; Singapore, for exam ple—continues to rise. This is both a
national and global challenge that we can and must rise  to, and that is why our
Government and I, as Minist er of Education, are focuse d on raising achievement for
every one of our children.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why does she continue to attribut e our drop in th e OECD rankings
to the rise of Asian countries, when New Zealand has been overtaken by other
countries—among them, Liechtenstein, Esto nia, Poland, Ireland, Be lgium, Germany,
Austria, Australia, Slovenia, Denmark—or perh aps we should focus a little bit more on
delivering a broad and balanced curriculum that might include things like geography?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Because, regrettably, this is a complex issue. Unfortunately
for the member, linear, single correlations do not actually work here. What the
Programme for International Student Assessment data tells us is that there are a range of
challenges, and we have a plan focusing on each and every one of them.
15208 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Dec 2013

items.text: I do not have to hand th e precise figure about the

New Zealand Defence Force—Joint Amphibious Task Force
9. JACQUI DEAN (National—Waitaki)  to the Minister of Defence : How have
recent New Zealand Defence Force exercises contributed toward the Government’s goal
of developing a Joint Amphibious Task Force?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The New Zealand
Defence Force recently completed Exercise Southern Katip ō, one of the largest military
exercises ever conducted—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I just need to stop the family chatter that is occurring
between both sides of the House. Could the Minister please start his answer again?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The New Zealand Defence Force recently
completed Exercise Southern Katip ō, one of the largest military exercises ever
conducted in New Zealand. This involved 2,200 military personnel from 10 countries.
The exercise tested the New Zealand Defen ce Force’s ability to mount a medium-scale
amphibious operation involving maritime, land, a nd air assets. I am pleased to advise
the House that the exercise demonstrated that the New Zealand Defence Force has made
great progress in build ing amphibious capability, and rema ins on track to have a fully
operational joint amphibious task force by 2015.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What is the value to New Zealand in the New Zealand Defence Force
developing a joint amphibious task force?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The Defence White Paper 2010  placed a
greater focus on security within our own region. Accordingly, the Defence Force turned
its focus towards developing th e capability to deliver hu manitarian assistance and
respond to security situations  in the South-west Pacific.  The ability to deploy land
forces across large stretches of ocean, by s ea or by air, and sustain those forces once
there, is therefore crucial to the New Zealand Defence Force.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What capability upgrades has the Government invested in to help
deliver the joint amphibious task force?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Recognising that amphibious operations would
require strength and capabilities, the G overnment has committed to a number of
capability purchases, including a new fleet of medium and heavy operational vehicles
capable of being deployed in medium and high threat environments, and an increased
number of upgraded Seasprite helicopters  with a range of upgraded avionics,
communications, radars, weapons, and other sy stems on board that are superior to the
existing fleet.

items.text: Does he believe that the asset sales programme has legitimacy,

items.text: Order! We have now got into the difficulty again of where we were,

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. This is a case that is from

items.text: Does he believe that the asset sales programme has legitimacy,

“Those donations were not expressly disclosed in the Return. Rather, they appear to

items.text: Yes. Parliament passed the legislation. The Supreme Court

items.text: Why did Treasury advise the G overnment in the Budget Policy
Statement that asset sales would increase the Government’s deficit, as measured by the

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think, as we have discussed in the House before, there are a
number of ways of measuri ng the impact of asset sales on the Government’s fiscal
balance. The calculations th at have been done under one version show it is mildly
positive, another version mildly negative, and a third version roughly neutral. As I
explained to the member this morning at the committee, the impact directly on the
Government’s balance was not the main driv er of the sales. The Government set out
subjectives for this process some time ago. The real  question now, t hough, is if the

items.text: I think the member’s question points to the problem with
those calculations, and that is  they are all hypothetical. For instance, if the Government
still owned those assets, the fact is we now know they would be worth considerably less

Government’s debt is at l east $4 billion lower than it ot herwise would be, but if the
Greens can get around to promising to buy the assets back—which you would think

Education Sector—Learning Media and Student Achievement
11. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Education

way of shares to a defunct, declining co mpany to pay Westpac over $4 million in debt

Housing—Homeownership, Affordability, and Supply
12. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atat ū) to the Minister of Housing : Does he

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I do. I stated that we needed to free

buyers, and we have doubled the number of  KiwiSaver first home deposits and trebled

order, and we have, this year, delivered on  our commitment to insulate every single

items.text: No, you cannot.

items.text: I can assure that member that this Government is very

items.text: I seek the leave of the House to table a document showing the
Minister that there was an earthquake in Christchurch.

items.text: I ask the member to use a bit of sense before he raises a point of

items.text: Why does he think that the Prime Minister told journalists that he was
tracking Auckland building consents week by week and that they were going up, and

areas legislation, already we have freed up another 5,000 sections. Before Christmas we

they opposed every single measure, such as the special housing ar eas legislation, that
will actually enable Auckland to build more houses?

Student Achievement—OECD Report

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from Ch ris Hipkins seeking to debate under
Standing Order 386 the release of the OECD  Programme for Inte rnational Student
Assessment 2012 data collection on the perf ormance of school students in reading,
literacy, maths, and science. The release of the results is a particular case of recent
occurrence. As an OECD study, there is no ministerial responsib ility for the data
released, but they de al with matters involving minist erial responsibility. The results
confirm a gradual decline in performance,  and echo findings from earlier studies.
Although that may represent an existing situation, the release of the OECD results is a
significant new occurrence of considerable pub lic interest. Educational achievement is
of fundamental importance. The public need  confidence in the G overnment’s response
and its education plan focus on a number of fronts to lift educat ional achievement in
order to give all young people a better ed ucation. I consider it important enough to
warrant the immediate attention of the House by way of an urgent debate.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I move, That the House take note of a
matter of urgent public importance. The public do indeed deserve to have confidence in
their Government’s education policies, but they cannot with this current Government.
What we have seen under this  current Government is that every time it has been called
upon to make decisions about education, it has consistently made the wrong call.
In the National Government’s first B udget, in 2009—its first Budget—it cut the
professional development funding for teacher professional development. It cut that by
$35 million. In the same Budget it gave another $36 million to private schools. That
says everything about this Government’s education priorities.
We should be concerned about the fall in  our OECD rankings. The Minister of
Education yesterday argued that this is an  ongoing trend. There was a modest decline in
2009. That modest decline has turned into a freefall under this Government. Our figures
have absolutely plunged. We have fa llen significantly, from seventh to 13 th in reading,
from seventh to 18 th in maths, and from 13 th to 23 rd in science. Those are significant
drops that have occurred under this National Government, and those are issues that we
should be very, very concerned about.
I have spent a lot of time going into schools ove r the last year and talking to teachers
about what is making a difference to them a nd why it is that our kids in our education
system are not achieving to the level that we  should be able to expect. What they are
saying quite clearly is that th is Government is so focused on constantly measuring the
problem, on constantly testing kids, that th e teachers have not actually got time any
more to teach the kids. The teachers want th is Government to remove the red tape so
that they can get on with the job they entered the teaching profession to do, which is to
15214 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
actually teach kids. What they are doing now is filling in forms to satisfy this National
Government. That is not leading to better educational outcomes for kids.
The studies that have been coming out in the last few days and weeks have clearly
shown that the Government’s education approa ch is absolutely failing. Let us look at
the New Zealand Council for Educational Rese arch’s report that came out last week.
Only 14 percent of principals—only 14 percent of principals—and 23 percent of
teachers say that national standards provide a valuable record of student learning. If
national standards are the Government’s fl agship education policy for lifting student
achievement, and yet the people who are being forced to implement them say they do
not work and they do not provide reliable info rmation, how is it that they are supposed
to lift student achievement? They simply  do not. Only 7 percent of principals—7
percent of principals—and 15 percent of t eachers believe that national standards are
robust. They are flimsy standards that are neither national no r standard—they are
neither national nor standard.
It is no wonder that this Government has got our schools and our teachers focused on
the wrong things. Hekia Parata, in her answ ers to questions toda y, talked about how
wonderful national standards were and how pa rents were so happy with the information
they were getting, and yet overwhelmingly parents are complaining that the information
they are getting as a result of national standards is inferior to the information they were
getting before national standards were introduc ed. Fifty-four percen t of parents did not
agree that national standards were providing a valuable record of students’ learning.
What was Hekia Parata’s response to that? It  was to attack the survey. Rather than
actually listen to what parent s are saying, Hekia Parata deci ded to instead attack the
survey, and, once again, she was totally wrong.
Sixty percent of teachers and 70 percent of  principals say that national standards
have created more work for little gain—more work for little gain. What that means is
that more of our teachers, more of our prin cipals, and more of the people who work in
schools every day with kids are spendi ng more time filling in forms for the
Government, constantly assessing kids but  not actually focusing on raising student
achievement, which is exactly where they should be focused. If a child comes to school
hungry, putting them on the scales every day to  see whether they have gained weight
simply will not work. The same principle app lies with their learning. If a child cannot
read at school, simply giving them the same  test every day to see whether they have
improved is not going to improve their ability to read. Giving them some additional
support so they can actually learn to read is what the Government should be focused on,
but it is not.
What it is busily devoting all of the reso urces in the education system towards is
implementing national standards. Of course, national standards, as  I said, are neither
national nor standard, so now the Government  is putting the money into trying to make
them more consistent. Well, again, maki ng the standards more consistent will not
improve student achievement. What it will do is put a whole lot more money and a
whole lot more time and energy in to a bur eaucratic exercise, rather than actually
focusing on lifting student achievement.
If we are going to get serious about lifting student achievement, why does the
Government not look at the things that actually work? Take Reading Recovery, a
programme that has establishe d credibility and that works.  The Labour Party has said
we will extend Reading Recovery  so kids who need that sup port will be able to get it.
That is actually a ve ry, very important and a very, ve ry sensible thing to do. Reading
Recovery says that if a child is falling be hind in their reading, they need intensive one-
on-one support—they need intensive one-on-one support. We cannot simply go to
teachers and say that if students are falling behind in their classes—and they have got
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15215
quite large classes—they can give all of the time they need to absolutely every student.
Sometimes some of those kids do need more intensive levels of support, and that is
where we should certainly be putting money. Th e Government is simply turning a deaf
ear to those concerns from teachers, principals, parents, and everyone else who is saying
they are not getting the support they need.
The Government says it needed national standards to identify where students were
falling behind so it could target the resources to deal with that. The problem is we
already knew where students were not achie ving. When National came into office in
2008, it talked about the areas where students were not achieving already and said that it
would do something about that. What it ha s done is spend its entire 5 years in
Government measuring the problem over a nd over again, and it has done nothing to
actually address the concerns and the issues.
What was National’s one solution? Let us go back. What was National’s one solution
in last year’s Budget? Its one solution in la st year’s Budget was to make class sizes
bigger. Hekia Parata’s best attempt at impr oving the quality of teaching and learning in
classrooms was to put more kids in front of every teacher—more kids in front of every
teacher. That is not going to improve student learning in New Zealand. Of course,
National was forced to back down because  every parent in the country understood
something that Hekia Parata and John Key di d not—that putting more kids in a class is
not going to allow the teacher more time—That  is right. Well, I will get on to private
and charter schools in a moment, Mrs King. It  is not going to allow the teachers more
time to spend with each child to focus on actually raising student achievement.
So where is the money going under this Government? Well, we have seen a
significant increase in funding for private schoo ls, and, of course, we have seen money
ploughed into that ideological experiment that the National Government would have us
believe was forced on it by that convicted criminal John Banks—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: —when he forced upon it the ch arter schools experiment, which
every credible academic doing research ha s argued will not work and will not lift
student achievement.
Let us go back to the OECD study. The OE CD study proved very, very clearly that,
in fact, when you control for socio-economic  factors, private sc hools do not do any
better than public schools do. And yet under this Government, because of its ideological
predisposition, we have seen significant amounts of extra m oney going into the private
schooling sector through private schools an d through charter schools. Actually, we
should be focusing on making sure every sc hool in New Zealand is a good school. The
Government has put in place Aspire Scholarsh ips so that it can send more kids into
private schools, and yet the results from th at are abysmal. The kids who are attending
private schools under those Aspire Scholar ships are not actually  achieving—they are
not achieving. It is not a good use of money.
We know the things that ar e working. If the Government  members actually took the
time to get out there and visit schools, to list en to teachers and principals, to listen to
parents, and to listen to the academic e xperts, they would actually know what is
working in schools. But they do not. They are completely deaf to the feedback that
educators are giving them. This is a Govern ment that has declared a war on teachers—a
war on teachers—because it believes that Na tional knows best. It believes that the
people who are in the classroom every day, teaching kids every day, do not know what
is going to raise student achievement and that  they have to be told by the National
Government what they need to do to rais e student achievement. Well, I tell you what. I
would put my money on a schoolteacher or a school principal knowing what is best for
the kids in their school far ahead of Hekia Parata’s knowledge of those issues. I trust the
15216 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
professional judgment of the people who are in our schools and who know how to raise
student achievement. That is not something they will get under this National
Government.
Let us look at Hekia Parata’s list of ex cuses for the decline in our OECD ranking,
because that is what they are—they are simply  excuses. First of all she talked about the
fact that we have had a “significant in crease in the number of teachers but under-
investment in raising teacher practice;”. Well, yes, we have had under-investment in
raising teacher practice, because this Govern ment cut the funding for that in its very
first Budget, in 2009. Coincidentally, that wa s the last time we had the Programme for
International Student Assessment results out . So we are seeing now, in the next
Programme for International Student Asse ssment study after the Government cut the
funding for teacher professional developmen t, what the impacts of those kinds of
Draconian policies are.
Other excuses from Hekia Parata include that there is “a focus on compliance rather
than … performance;”, and yet national standards are all about compliance. That is what
this Government is focused on. It is all about compliance and—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Bureaucracy gone mad.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: —bureaucracy gone mad—tying sch ools and teachers up in red
tape, and not trusting them to make judgments  about what is best for students. It is
about making them fill in forms to satisfy this quest of the Government to rank
everything and to have league tables, ra ther than focusing on teaching the whole
curriculum, which is where our schools shoul d really be focused. Hekia Parata said
there is “Inadequate … data on student achievement …”. That is absolute nonsense. We
have always had very good da ta on student achievement. Wh at we have not been good
at doing as a system is matching the additi onal resources to wher e student achievement
is failing. This Government has been among the worst because what it has been doing is
cutting the funding to programmes that have targeted areas of underachievement.
We in the Labour Party recognise the links  between inequality in our society and
under-performance in the education system . That is something to which this
Government turns a blind eye and a deaf ear . This is a Government that refuses to
measure child poverty—refuses to even  measure child poverty. And yet we
acknowledge that the conditions that kids are growing up in have an impact on their
readiness to learn when they get to school —something that the National Government is
simply not willing to hear.
This is a wake-up call to the Governmen t; its education policies are failing. Other
countries that have experienced a similar d ecline in the education rankings are taking
that very, very seriously. They are willing to reassess and re-examine the policies they
have put in place that are not working. So why is our Government trying to continue to
push along the policies that have been proven to fail? They have been proven to fail,
and that is exactly what is happening with th is Government. It is arrogant and out of
touch. As in so many other areas, this Government is not listening to the people whom it
is relying on every day in schools to get out in front of kids, to teach kids. It is not
listening to them.
The first thing this Government should do is  admit that it is wrong. Then it should
actually go out there and say to teachers and principals: “Actually, we think that you are
professionals. We actually trus t your judgment. What is it that we need to do as a
Government to lift student achievement?”. That  is the very first thing this Government
should do. But we will not get that from He kia Parata, because Hekia Parata knows
best. Instead, she will go a nd lecture schools about all of th e things that they are doing
wrong and about whether they are pronouncing their kids’ names right, but she will not
actually put the effort, the energy, and the resources into areas where we know that kids
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15217
are not achieving. Instead, National wants to import failed ideological experiments from
overseas. It is no surprise that other countries that have adopted standardised assessment
and standardised testing are either stagnati ng or declining in the education rankings, as
well.
What we need to be doing is embracing the whole curric ulum. We have one of the
best curricula in the world. It  is internationally recognised.  It was put in  place by the
previous Labour Government. I will say that it was put in place by the previous Labour
Government, but it was supported by the th en National Opposition. National was right
then; what it has done instead since it cam e into Government is undermine the world-
leading curriculum that we have. It has undermined that consistently by saying to
teachers and to schools that it does not want  them teaching the whole curriculum; it
wants them to focus on only a narrow range of things. That is not going to lead to a
more prosperous future for our country. Th e OECD statistics that  are out this week
show that the Government’s education policies are failing.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I am
delighted to be able to participate in this  debate because, despite the hysterical tone
being adopted by the Opposition member Chris Hipkins, New Zealand has a
fundamentally sound education system. I have  said since I became the Minister of
Education that the system is top performi ng for many, but not for all. That has not
happened by accident, nor will  it continue without attenti on, and this Government is
paying attention. Ever since I became the Minister, it has be en paying attention. Unlike
the assertion by the Opposition member that this is a wake-up call, it is not. Our alarm
clock rang 5 years ago when we looked at the system we had inherited from those
people who are now on the other side, and that is why we got straight into fixing this.
We knew that we had to understand exactly where every child was in our system in
order to be able to target resources specifically to them, to help address their learning
needs right there and then, a nd not wait for 3-year sample s that, yes, are extremely
helpful and inform our decision making. But it is a call to action. As I said in my speech
to the Iwi Chairs Forum last week, to whic h the forum responded magnificently, this is
an endeavour that all of us need to be engaged in. That means that we need to know
where our kids are at in the system, what th eir particular learning needs are, whether we
have the resources to suppor t them, and how we can make a difference for each and
every one of them.
New Zealand has slipped in the latest  Programme for International Student
Assessment rankings. This is serious, but it is not a surprise. We are serious about fixing
this. That is why our plan is about every part of the education system.
At early childhood, about which all the resear ch is really clear, investing early is
investing for life. That is why we have—despite the Opposition ignoring the brutal facts
of reality—raised investment in early ch ildhood education by 74 percent. The reason
why we have invested in this is that we trust parents as much as professionals. There are
many parents who deliver great early childhood  learning to their ch ildren in their own
homes, as do qualified teachers in centres. We are agnostic as to which choice parents
make. It is up to parents to decide how and where to send their children for early
childhood education. If that is at home with their parents, we applaud that. If that is in a
teacher-led centre, whether kindergarten or kōhanga reo, we applaud that.
This Government has focused on having a target of 98 percent of our earliest learners
participating in early chil dhood education, and we are now  at 95.8 percent. We will
keep on focusing on what works for commun ities. So whether that is a Pasifika
language - led playgroup or a kindergarten, we will support those earliest learners to
have that opportunity.
15218 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
When children enter school, we want them to develop a strong general platform in
primary school. We want it understood whether or  not they are able to read, write, and
count at the earliest age, and we want to  make a difference as  soon as we understand
whether that is occurring or not.
We have invested $9.7 billi on in Vote Education this year alone, and we have
increased that investment every year be cause we understand how important and how
critical education is to every one of our children. It has not been acceptable to us that an
average of four out of five children l eave senior secondary school with National
Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 2. When we came into
Government, it was two out of five M āori and three out of five  Pasifika. We are not
looking at averages and, in fact, we have raised achievement ever since 2009.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: No, it’s going backwards.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I get that the members opposite,  and one in particular, are
not interested in reality or facts or evid ence, but we have actually had improvements
year on year. How do we know that? It is be cause we have invested in a data-rich
environment. We understand that without data it is just another person’s opinion.
We are interested in data and in making a difference. That is why we introduced
national standards. Every parent and teacher  wanted to know specifically where their
child was once every 3 years but also every y ear and every 6 months , which is what is
required under this Government. But they can also find out how their child is doing in
national standards at any time. We are not asking teachers, as has been asserted by the
Opposition, to do more assessment. We are as king them to use their overall teacher
judgment to make a decision as to how well their children are doing and what we need
to do next to improve that, and to ensure th at their parents unders tand, because parents
want the best for their children and they want  to be involved in helping their children to
improve.
I do go out to schools. In fact, I have a very structured 40 Friday programme,
because there are 40 Fridays in a school year . I am in schools every Friday somewhere
around the country. I listen to what teachers ha ve to say and I take action as a result of
that.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: It’s no wonder they’re going backwards.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Most recently—if the member cared to listen instead of
haranguing from that side of the House—it wa s said that professional learning was not
meeting their particular needs, so I have introduced a review. We heard that teachers
required more maths and science resources, so we have invested in that.
We know that kids do better if they particip ate early. We know that kids do better if
their parents are engaged. We know that kids do better if the comm unity in which their
school is located holds high expectations of and for them. So this year, for the first time,
we have published by local authority and rohe  the specific achievement of kids so that
those communities can join together in raising achievement for each and every one of
them.
The 4,000 15-year-olds who sat the Programme for International Student Assessment
last year showed that our best are still best in the world but also that our least capable
students are some of the lowest in the Pr ogramme for International Student Assessment
countries. Our spread between those who ar e doing very well and those who are not is
one of the widest in the OECD, and we are focused on how we get excellence and
equity for all. Unfortunately, these kids—these 4,000 kids—were not caught by national
standards, but they have been caught by our Youth Guarantee initiative, by the fees-free
places in tertiary institutions, by the incr eased number of apprenticeships, and by the
vocational pathways that offer opportunities to kids in the primary sector, in the services
sector, in manufacturing, in health, and, s hortly, in the creative industries. They will
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15219
also have greater focus on NCEA level 2, a nd we are working with schools, school by
school, on how we raise that achievement.
We are prioritising parents by better re porting to them. We are providing better
information for the wider community. We are putting more funding into the New
Zealand School Trustees Association, which is the most formal and structured way in
which over 16,000 people—mainly parents—volunteer every 3 years to be on the
boards of our schools. We have had an 84 percent increase in its funding this year.
The biggest effect on in-school raising ach ievement is the quality of teaching and
education leadership, and we have invested $37.5 million this year in a quality teaching
agenda. The cornerstone of that is the transformation of the New Zealand Teachers
Council into the Education Council of Aotearoa New Zealand. Its acronym is
EDUCANZ, not “Edu-can’t”, so we can ensure that the professional body of teachers is
fit for the 21 st century. We are also introducing, from next year, initial teacher
qualifications that strike a much stronger balance between educat ion theory and great
classroom practice. We have introduced excell ence awards because we want to be able
to highlight and spotlight to  the community what excellenc e looks like. There are many
examples of that up and down the country , where teachers are creating magic in
classrooms every day with their students. We want to highlight that.
Most particularly, we want to create a more constructiv e public conversation around
education. We want to be able to attract the best and brightest to join the profession. If
all they ever hear is binary, oppositional statements about edu cation, then why would
they be attracted to doing that? So we are investing next year in education—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: You cut the funding for teachers in early childhood.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: The member keeps parroting that we have cut the funding.
How can you have a 74 percen t increase in early childhood education and a 40 percent
increase in schooling and say that it constitute s a cut? It just does not  bear scrutiny. It is
laughable, frankly. It is just absolutely ridiculous. In fact, it is an example of exactly
what I have just been alluding to. We ca nnot get a constructive education conversation
in this country. Until we grow up and start having a constructive—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: —a constructive—education co nversation, it will be very
difficult to persuade young people to choose teaching as a career.
I grew up in a community where teachers we re revered. I was really proud that my
father was one of those teachers, and I am pr oud that my sisters joined the profession. I
am proud of all the people I know who have committed their lives to this vocation of
teaching. That is why we have invested $9.7 billion—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Why do you denigrate them as union hacks, then?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Actually, I do not denigrate teachers, at all.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: You do.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I do not denigrate teachers, at all. Can I just—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: They shouldn’t have an opinion—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member can take a call shortly.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes, that would be great.
Can I just speak to the particular issu e of pronouncing children’s names correctly.
Can we start with the fact that mine is  Hekia Parata, and can we recognise that
relationships of respect established betw een 5-year-olds and the teacher, between 10-
year-olds and the teacher, and between 15-y ear-olds and the teacher actually do start
with pronouncing a child’s name correctly, whet her it is Mary-Anne or Mereana. I do
not see why that should send anyone into a frenzy. It is a basic, common courtesy.
So we are working really hard, and the reason we are doing so is that we want—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I thought it was Trish.
15220 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes, it is, and I am not hung up about that, because I am a
comfortable bicultural New Zealander. Nō te mea he ingoa tipuna tēnā nō aku tīpuna.
[Because that is an ancestral name from my ancestors.]
Ko Patricia i heke mai i aku t īpuna n ō K ōtimana. Ko taku ingoa a Hekia he ingoa
tipuna nō Ngāti Porou.
[Patricia comes from my Scottish ances tors. My name Hekia is an ancestral name
from Ngāti Porou, the clan or tribe of Porou.]
So, yes, I am Patricia Hekia Parata. I am proud of both sides of my heritage: P ākehā
and Māori. I think many New Zealand kids are.
So we want to have an education system  that makes our children competitive both
internationally and globally and that also em braces those things that are uniquely New
Zealand. Our kids—and these things ar e not measured by the Programme for
International Student Assessment—are good at working in teams. Our kids are good at
finding creative and innovative solutions to  problem solving. Our kids are good at
relationships. Our kids are good in the environment. Our kids are committed to fairness
and sportsmanship. We want to have an edu cation system that is about kids both being
globally competitive and having that Kiwi, can-do attitude, which is unique to New
Zealand. I am bound and determined that th e New Zealand education system will
deliver both of those opportunities to every one of our children.
I am proud to be the Minister of Educati on in the National Government, raising the
vote investment every year, committed to modernising our education system, and
making some people uncomfortable with chan ge, because if we keep doing what we
have always done, we will keep getting what we have always got. What we have always
got has not been good enough, so we are facing forwards, informed by what has
happened in the past, but really focused on what makes a differenc e. Funnily enough,
opinion and prejudice are outweighed by evidence and research.
Thank you, Mr Speaker, for giving me the oppor tunity, despite the haranguing of the
parrots on the other side—the Op position—to talk about all the great things we have in
our education system and also how much better we need to be doing.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā koutou i te
Whare. It is very, very pleasi ng to be part of this urgent debate, and very interesting. I
listened closely to the Minister of Education. I think that there are many parents in this
country who would love to see all of us in  this House working together on education.
But there are some fundamental problems, a nd the Programme for International Student
Assessment report actually highlights those pr oblems. It talks about  slippage. It talks
about slippage, and it also does a very inte resting analysis of why the direction the
Government has taken education policy in is not going to work.
I want to quote A ndreas Schleicher—[Interruption] I am sure you will, Minister. I
am sure you will quote him. He is quoted as saying, when he unveiled the international
student assessment results: “My organisation is very strong on choi ce, enabling citizens
to make choices, and you would expect that  systems with the greatest choice would
come out better … You expect competition to  raise performance of the high performers
and with low performers put them out of the market. But in fact you don’t see that
correlation … Competition alon e is not a predictor for better outcomes. The UK is a
good example—it has a highly competitive school  system but it is still only an average
performer.”

items.speaker: Others have said
items.text: “His comments could be seen as a blow for Michael Gove,
England’s education secretary, who has placed great importa nce on the findings of Pisa
and has also promoted increased school choi ce as a key way of raising educational
standards. This has been done  in England through more academies and the introduction
of state-funded free schools,”—also known as  charter schools—“par tly inspired by the
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15221
charter schools in the US.” Andreas Schleich er is quoted as saying:  “Our data does not
show much of a performance difference …” . So what Andreas Schleicher from the
Programme for International St udent Assessment is saying is that the direction that the
Government is trying to take the education system in is not going to work.
That is why, as deeply as the Green Party would like to get past ideological battles in
binary opposition and start focusing on the best, most innovative, most creative, and
most culturally inclusive school system in the world, we have a problem in this political
situation. That problem is that choice does not work in education. If you are talking
about why achievement is sli pping and why we have gone down in maths, science, and
literacy or reading in the report’s figures , it is because a programme based upon
increased choice and teaching to tests cannot deliver what the Government says it wants
to deliver for all children. Therefore, th e Green Party has many, many other ideas that
