would be more positive.
But it is really important to think about  the Programme for International Student
Assessment and what its report said in this round, because the report is talking about the
last 3 years and it is talking about our country being in a state of failure. It is a wake-up
call. It is not actually something the Govern ment should be making light of or walking
away from and saying that it  is an ongoing problem that it  was well aware of. I have
never heard the Government admit that choice is not going to work.
The report says, and this is one of the thin gs that I find interest ing, that one of the
most important things is professional development. I heard the Minister say on Morning
Report that she is doing everything that th e programme suggested. But actually she is
not, because the cuts to science advisers a nd to professional development in science
have been a disaster. I am sure I am not the only MP in  this House who has received
emails from science advisers, drama advise rs, and cultural advisers saying: “We have
lost jobs, but that is not the only issue for us. What is happeni ng is that the broad
curriculum, which we are only just rolli ng out, is being undermined and narrowed
because we are not getting the professional development to allow our teachers to do the
magic that they are supposed to do.” So this  is a direct contradi ction between what the
Minister said on Morning Report , that she is fulfilling all of the programme’s
suggestions, and the reality that instead of greater professional development and a broad
curriculum, less choice but more focus on lo cal quality public education will get better
outcomes for all.
The report’s information is worth reading because it talks about the importance of
universalism and it talks about the importanc e of quality teaching and attracting quality
teachers. No one is going to disagree with th at. But the problem we have got is that the
plan that the Government is rolling out in this country at the moment will not deliver
those outcomes. That plan is all about natio nal standards, which is called teaching to
test, and they are neither national nor standard.
If you read the latest research that cam e out last week, you will find that the New
Zealand Council for Educational Research an d Martin Thrupp’s st udy both raised red
flags about what is happening with national standards. They are very concerned about
the narrowing of the curriculum. That is why the Programme for International Student
Assessment results have to be taken in the context of what is not working in this
country. What is not working is measuring the cow, not feeding the cow. There are
many ways we could say that.
But the Government is not listening to teachers, parents, and principals. Seven
percent of principals in th e Council for Educational Rese arch study said that national
standards could be considered to be robust. That is 93 percent who said they could not
be considered as robust—93 percent of principa ls in the study said that they could not
consider the standards to be robust. What we have, with that kind of statistic, is
15222 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
evidence that one cannot build a political consensus if the teaching profession, the
principals, and, indeed, many parents are d eeply unhappy with the strategies that the
Government has brought in since 2008, which are not strategies fo r promoting a broad
curriculum, individual learning plans, and success for all students.
I heard the Minister list all the wonderful things that the Government is doing. I have
heard her talk about those in glowing term s. But, unfortunately, the slippage and
particularly the socio-economic data that is in the report show that the context in which
the Government is trying to promote the gl obal education reform  movement is not
working for it. That is why in the st udent assessment study the programme has
identified this country as failing on socio-economic disadvantage strategies.
The programme is saying that we are not  doing enough for the vulnerable students,
whether it is through providing them with fo od, as my colleague Hone Harawira has
promoted through his bill, or whether it is through providing them with a broad
curriculum with better cultura l inclusion strategies, more qualified teachers, and better
early childhood education instead of cutting th e ratios, which is what the Government
has done to the qualifications of early child hood teachers. It cannot keep putting up
these contradictions. On the one hand we have heard the Minister say that early
childhood education is wonderful, but on the ot her hand the Government is going to cut
the target of having 100 percent register ed teachers. That is an unbelievable
contradiction. If you talk to the early chil dhood sector, it is deep ly distressed by what
has happened as a result of that strategy.
Moving on to the compulsory sector, we  have the collapse of professional
development and the introduction of the most  unpopular policies th at the Government
could get through. The Government could not get class sizes through, so it continued
with national standards. Teacher s are regularly telling me thi ngs like that one school is
writing in school reports “working toward s the standard” but another school is
describing it as “well below”. There is nothing consistent or standard about the way that
schools are describing these measures that th ey are supposed to im pose. Some schools
are actually doing two reports. They are doing one report for national standards and they
are doing another report for what the parents actually want to know about their kids.
But I want to talk briefly, in the time I have left in this urgent debate, about
educational solutions. The Green Party is to tally passionate about creating solutions.
Tomorrow I am hosting a forum at Parliament , in the theatrette, and you are all invited.
I have some of the most innovative and creative people coming to talk about the
solutions that the Green Party and others have  to make sure this country works better.
They are going to be about facing up to  equity, about stopping the teach-to-test
mentality, and about introducing and supporting professional development for the broad
curriculum. They are going to be about looki ng at schools being genuinely accessible to
all children, and genuinely free. These people whom I have brought together for
tomorrow are about finding solutions to th e challenges that the Programme for
International Student Assessment has put out.
I think it is an important duty of all pol iticians—but particularly of the Greens
because we actually think posit ive solutions and a fairer future are important for all
children—that we start articulating what will work. The report from the Programme for
International Student Assessment and the quot e from Andreas Schleicher that I just
gave from show that inequality is a funda mental issue. Unlike many other countries in
the study, New Zealand’s results are getting worse. We have had in the last 5 years a
serious increase in inequality and socio-ec onomic disadvantage in terms of education.
The OECD is being quite brave, because it has always been a grea t believer in choice,
but it is now admitting that choice is failing. It is brave enough to admit that we actually
need different strategies.
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15223
So tomorrow we are going to be talking a bout some of those strategies, including
things like early childhood education, in the language of the sector’s own people. I look
forward to talking about this further with you. We need positive solutions. We need a
fair future and a good life for all our kids . We do not need the current Government’s
strategies.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Can I first of all thank you,
Mr Speaker, for allowing this debate to go forward, because this is something of full
concern to the country. It is a matter of gr eat urgency. However, the first comments I
want to make are that, unfor tunately, statements that th e Minister of Education has
made today and the Prime Minister made yest erday show the ignorance that they have
about the current system. Both the Minist er and the Prime Minister have made
statements that these children were not cap tured by national standards and that these
children were not inside that system from  2008 forward. In 2008 this cohort, which is
my son’s cohort, were actually in year 7. Y ear 7 and year 8 are primary school children.
They were inside the national standards system.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: They were not. They were introduced in 2010.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: These children were primary school children at year 7 and
year 8. They were covered by the primary school New Zealand curriculum and they
were captured by national standards.
At the same time as this Government cam e in—and I note that Minister Anne Tolley
is there, because it was Minister To lley who brought nationa l standards in and
campaigned against teachers in 2008, the most  vicious campaign against the teachers of
New Zealand that has ever been seen. The devaluing that that Minister and this
Government did in 2008 to the morale of our teaching community has never been seen
before.
These teachers today, our teachers today, are the most undervalued and the most
under attack as has ever been seen in our natio n’s history. It is a shame that that is the
National Government, which created the worl d-leading New Zealand curriculum in full
consultation—in full consultation—with the sector and with total agreement with all
parties inside this House and with every te acher who had to implement it. That was the
way under the guidance of the Hon Dr Lock wood Smith—that was the way. If that was
where we needed to go as a c ountry, that is how it should have been  done. But it was
not done that way. There was an arrogant  solution from behind closed doors by a
Government that was trying to play up for a vote in 2008.
I was sitting on the board of trustees of Warkworth Primary School in 2008. I sat on
that board with some parents who wanted to  bring back ranking inside our classrooms.
National standards are about as close as you can get without going back to ranking of
students inside classrooms. It is the ranking of  schools inside league tables, and it is the
pressure of competition to try to create better outcomes instead of actually deciding to
invest in professional development.
I want to take up the point that the Minister has made  about the pronunciation of
children’s names. I absolutely agree with her. But why, then, does the Minister continue
to argue against compulsory professional deve lopment? Why is it that if we proved that
the Te Kotahitanga programme had maximum outcomes for M āori students, we did not
make it compulsory for every teacher in th is country to take that professional
development? Why is it that if we need to  have our teachers in our classrooms—and,
interestingly enough, we are importing them fr om other nations. We are not saying that
they have to take any professional devel opment about our culture, about our languages,
and about the way New Zealanders are and the nuances that we have with our young
people. We place them in front of the classroom . Why is it that this Minister says that
professional development must remain contes table? It makes no sense to New Zealand
15224 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
First that if you have a teaching fraternity who you say must take professional
development, why you do not make it compulsory and why you do not fund it
appropriately.
We also reiterate that we agree with the Minister. We knew where these children
were. It is interesting that the catchphrase at the moment for this Government is “a data-
rich environment”. Why is it, then, that school  entry data is not captured? Why is it that
school entry data—knowing where these children are when they actually come in to the
school, predominantly at 5, even though the law says that they do not have to enter our
schools until 6—is not being captured? Why is it, then, when we already knew that we
had children requiring Reading Recovery—and let us be clear  that Reading Recovery is
for those children who need that  little push to get over the li p of their difficulty in order
to be at the same place as their peers—that we still ha ve Reading Recovery funding
based on a decile rating? A d ecile 8 school gets funded fo r half a child no matter how
many children actually require Reading Recove ry. If we are front -ending the spend,
why are we not putting that funding for that ch ild as soon as we know that they need
assistance? We already knew that, but that is not what is ha ppening—that is not what is
happening. Children are being id entified as needing that support of Reading Recovery.
At Warkworth Primary School 12 children get id entified, say, in a y ear, and the school
gets funding for half a child. So what does the school have to do? It has to fund-raise to
try to put in that support for those childre n—and these are 5-year-olds and 6-year-olds
we are talking about—or it needs to take from  its operations grant or it does not provide
it.
If the Minister and this Government were truly invested in li fting and front-ending
the spend and lifting the perf ormance of these young people so  that by the time they
enter the Programme for International Student Assessment exams they have that solidity
of foundation, those two questions need to  be answered. Why should professional
development be contestable? And why are we not providing the support for a child as
soon as it is identified, and it is identified under the assessments that have not changed?
The other part to this and why it is important is that this is our international
reputation. We try to sell our education system overseas. So of course it is a great
concern to everybody in this House, to ev erybody in New Zealand, and, I would have
thought, predominantly to thos e schools that are over ther e now, marketing themselves
for international students to come here because we have such a great education system.
This is of concern.
When the Minister talks about growi ng up and people having a cross-party
consensus, my experience in the 2 years that I have been in this House is that, actually,
it is the National Party that never shows up. It is the National Party that never enters the
conversation. I have been invited over the last 2 years to education panel after education
panel, and there has been no National Party re presentative there. I take that back. Cam
Calder—and Mr Ngaro, though that was actually something about social services, not
education necessarily—came to the adult and community education panel and read
statements from the Government. New Zealand First would love to have an opportunity
to gather together all members in this H ouse who are concerned about education, take
the politics out of the room, and bring in the Principals’ Federation, the New Zealand
Educational Institute, and the Post Primary Teachers Association. They care about these
children. What about the boards of trustees? There are the pa rents. There is your parent
body that you should bring into the room.

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: They’re not all parents.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: But, apparently, Miss Collins, we do not provide them with
compulsory professional development, either. The Minister quite incorrectly stated that
they were volunteers. These people are el ected officials from their communities. The
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15225
parents who sit on the boards of trustees have been elected from their parental
community. Only the parental community can vote for them, and that is how they gain a
seat. You have to have a chil d inside the school to be able  to vote for anybody to be on
to the board of trustees.

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: Not to be a trustee.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Miss Collins obviously need s to go back and study the
Education Act 1989, because she is completely mistaken around her abilities. The
boards of trustees are the pare ntal voice out of those communities and they should be in
the room. Too often they have been ignor ed not only by this Government but by the
education sector itself. It is those people w ho should also have compulsory professional
development. Some money has been placed aside, and I commend the Minister for
actually placing that money with the School Tr ustees Association, but we still have not
recognised that these are the leaders of our  schools. We still do not acknowledge that it
is through their work and their leadership th at they represent that community and the
outcomes that that community chooses for its children. We must widen the success
criteria, not narrow the success criteria, so th at all our children can succeed inside the
current State school system. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak
in this debate. I think I share with many me mbers in this House the concern about the
Programme for International St udent Assessment results. The first thing that I want to
say is that every week I visit schools, I meet parents, I meet teachers, I meet principals,
and I meet people who are absolutely passionate about our education system. But I think
it is really important that when we enter this debate, we actually analyse what the
Programme for International Student Assessmen t is telling us. There are a number of
very clear things coming through from this report.
The first thing that I want to address is that we have had a number of things raised by
the Opposition that are just not  true. The first thing that we  heard from Labour was that
these results were actually because National had under-invested in our education
system. Well, this is not true. We ar e spending $9.7 billion—the highest ever
investment in Vote Education—with year-o n-year increases. There has been a 40
percent increase in Vote Education since 2007. We are investing 20 percent of all public
expenditure in education, which is the second highest in the OECD.
The second thing that we heard from Mr Hi pkins was that this was actually all our
fault. Well, actually, when you look at th e Programme for International Student
Assessment results, the real ity is that these children  came through between 2003 and
2012. What we need to do in this House is ac tually stop the blame game and accept that
this is a serious issue, that it needs proper analysis, and that it is  an education system
issue, and all members of the House need to  band together to act ually look at how we
address some of these issues.
The third thing we heard was that the reason for these Programme for International
Student Assessment results was actually nati onal standards—I know that we have just
heard from Tracey Martin on that—but, actually, that is factually untrue. National
standards were introduced in 2010. The reality is that the children in this cohort could
not benefit from the targeting of national standards—knowing where children needed to
be lifted—because national standards were  not properly implemented through that
period. They were introduced in 2010 and childre n could not have been targeted in that
2003 to 2012 period.
The next thing that we heard was that this  is actually somehow because of charter
schools and investment in private educat ion. Again, I think many New Zealanders
listening to this debate would realise that that is ridiculous.
15226 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
So now we actually get to the point where we can ask what is going on here. I think
that the most important thing that we need to  remember is that for the last decade there
has been a group of voices in th is country that has said “We need change.”, right? Then
there has been a group of other voices that has said “No, we need no change.” It has
been our Government and our party that have been consistent in saying that actually the
only way that we can ensure that every child gets the kind, of opportunities that we want
for every New Zealander is to have change . That is why we are unashamedly proud of
national standards.
The biggest thing that I say to many audien ces, and to many teachers, principals, and
parents when I get out in the community, is: “How can we possibly help those children
if we don’t know where they are and we don’t know where we can help them?”. It is so
simple. The reality is that now we do know where those children are and we are putting
in resources to help them.
The second thing that we have really focu sed on is recognising that we do need to
ensure that we raise the value of the teach ing profession. That is about professional
development. We did announce a review this  week, and that is going to be very
important in terms of raising the value of  the profession and ra ising quality teaching.
The next thing that we have done is that we ha ve been really clear that the reform of the
Teachers Council is incredibly important to en sure that the teaching profession as well
has greater responsibility and a greater role in terms of lifting standards.
I think there has traditionally been a problem in New Zealand in terms of truancy and
school-leavers. The other thing that th e Programme for International Student
Assessment results show, which I think is re ally interesting, is that more kids are
staying at school, which is great. Early leavi ng exemptions fell to 313 last year from a
peak of more than 4,187 applications in 2005. That is a 93 per cent decrease under
National. That is incredibly significant because how can we possibly improve our
education system and raise opportunities for young people if they are not actually at
school? I think there are some quite amazing re sults here in terms of areas like school-
leavers.
There are some other very positive things happening in terms of national standards
and professional development, but all people in this House need to realise that this is
serious, and the only way that we can really do service to the rest of New Zealand is by
taking responsibility and making change.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: There can be no surer sign that you
have got a Government that is on the run fr om its own record in education when you
have the Minister of Education and an Associate Minister of Education stand up and say
that we need to take the politics out of e ducational achievements—this from a party that
campaigned hard to get into Government  in 2008 on its headline policy of national
standards. Well, National, you have failed your standards in  education. This is a fail
grade for what National is doing to our education system.
This report is seriously concerning for New Zealand. It  has shown The programme
for International Assessment that there are systemic failures within our education
system, which are being exacerbated by the introduction of national standards. The
dramatic drop that we have seen in the in ternational standing of our education system
should be a real wake-up call to the Nationa l Government. Its approach is simply not
working, and the mad spinning to try to explain this away does nothing for our children,
who are being failed by a Government that is  systemically chipping away at what was
once a world-class education system with a world-class curriculum and world-class
teachers. This is being undermined by our own Government.
National’s attacks on education have seen our overall rankings fall. Let us go back
and think about those numbers again: from seventh to 18 th in science, from 13 th to 23rd
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15227
in maths, and from seventh to 13 th in reading. This is from a Government that talks the
big game on innovation. We have Minister  Joyce standing up time and time again and
telling us that the salvation for the New Zealand economy is going to be innovation, led
by world-class science. Well, here is a revelation, Government: if you want an
innovation-led economy that relies heavily on  the sciences, you need to have our
students performing at a world-class level in  science and mathematics. You do not have
them sliding down the OECD rankings and thin king that we can be a country that can
perform on the international stage as a globa l innovator. It simply does not work. The
maths does not compute.
We had the Minister of Education stand up and say that her Government is one that
is interested in data, and an Associate Minist er who said that we need to analyse. So I
will put it together again for the Minister an d the Associate Minister. Here is some data
for you to analyse. In 2000 New Zealand wa s seventh in the OECD in mathematics.
After your Government made its changes, we are now 23rd in the OECD.
Let us analyse that data, Government, and see where you come to. Let us look at
science, for a Government that is supposedly committed to a science and innovation-led
economy. In 2000 we were seventh in the OECD . After this Government has been in
power for 5 years, in 2013 we have slid down the rankings to 18th.
What we have is a Government that has systemically chipped away at science within
our education system. We have a Government that thought it was a smart move to cut
technology funding in the 2012 Budget. The G overnment had to back-pedal on it
because its own voters told it that it was a dumb idea. This is not a Government that
matches its rhetoric on innovation with what it is doing in our education system. This is
a Government that cut $35 million out of professional development for our teachers in
Budget 2009. Yet the Minister will stand up and berate us with the fact that we need our
teachers to continue learni ng. Yes, we do, and the Minist er slicing off $35 million,
which saw the demise of science advisers in  schools, is not the way that New Zealand
can have an innovation-led future.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: That was a very—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have not called the
member yet. The member must wait to be called. I call the honourable member Dr Cam
Calder.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: No member of this House can take pleasure in these
Programme for International Student Assessment results. It is a serious concern, but the
Labour Party and its union cronies can ha ve nothing to be proud of—nothing to be
proud of. Dr Megan Woods mentioned 2000. You got your statistics wrong. You got
your statistics wrong—2000 was after 9 years of a National Government where our
successive Ministers of Educat ion were relentlessly critic ised by the Labour Party and
its union acolytes for our education policy.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Ten seconds to denigrate teachers.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It was after 9 years of a National Government that we had
these statistics: third in the world for reading, fourth in the world for maths, and seventh
in the world for science, Dr Megan Woods . There was a steady decline from 2000 to
2009 where Labour did absolute ly nothing, nada, null, zer o. It was seduced by the
education unions’ sibilant assurances and w easel words that all was right with the
education sector, that nothing needed to change, and, sadly, we have heard that again
from the Opposition speakers. Labour was blinkered and steadfastly ignored the
growing disparity between our best students, where we were  up there with the rest of
the world, and our poorly performing student s and the relative underachievement of our
Māori and Pasifika students.
15228 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
After National came into office, New Zealand’s rating in 2009, after the supervised
neglect, showed seventh for reading, 13th for maths, and seventh for science. You would
think that, well, that is ostensibly not bad,  but let us disaggregat e them as we did.
Disaggregated for reading, P ākehā are second, Asians are seventh, M āori are 34th equal
between Slovenia and Slovakia, and Pasifika are down there at 44th, around Mexico. We
saw this information. We actually thought about it, interpreted the results, and knew that
this disparity and inequity were unacceptable,  as was the decline. We set about doing
something about it. Sadly, the unions continued to cry that all was well, aided and
abetted by their Labour Party cronies, and fe rociously fought and continue to fight
every single measure that this perceptive National Government has introduced to arrest
the decline and turn it round.
The 2012 Programme for International Stude nt Assessment results are a saddening
vindication of what we alre ady knew about student achievement in New Zealand and
have been working to address. That is, our  highest-achieving students are comparable
with those in the rest of the world. Howeve r, the whole education system needs to be
better geared for all students to succeed, and it is wrong and foolish to believe that just
the education unions know how to do this. If they knew how to do it, why are we in the
state we are in? As we have been saying fo r the last 5 years, our education is not
performing for all, and we ar e relentlessly focusing on refi ning it and ensuring that our
work raises achievement for five out of five of our students so that they can unlock that
potential that lies w ithin themselves. This was a well- signposted decline, and it is
appropriate and relevant to note that the 15-year-olds tested will not have benefited
from many of the innovations that we have introduced. I am , of course, talking about
national standards, the progress and consis tency tool, and the Positive Behaviour for
Learning programme, which this Government has introduced. Of co urse, those tested
would not have benefited from the $1.5 billi on assigned to early childhood education.
Successful education, of necessity, must be  infinitely varied in its engagement
strategies. No one size fits all.
This Government is ahead of the game, and the multiple new strands in the cable of
educational pathways we have introduced wi ll help turn round th is observed inherited
decline in Programme for International St udent Assessment performance. Our goal of
98 percent participation in early childhood e ducation will ensure that our young people
will get the best start, and our  current rate of participati on of 95.8 percent is the highest
ever. National standards will mean that teachers and parents can intervene early when
their children, and our children, are fall ing behind. As I said, the progress and
consistency tool, PaCT, will be a huge he lp, enabling teachers  to deepen their
understanding of the New Zealand curriculum, know how their students are progressing,
and know how they might support each individual student, and, indeed, it will provide
detailed reporting to parents with examples  and help engage students themselves in
directing their own learning.
Lifting the achievement level of National Certificate of Educational Achievement
(NCEA) level 2—the numbers achieving at that level—will be important. The transition
into further education and employment for mo st of our young people will be helped by
that. In 2012, 74 percent of our  school-leavers left with NCEA level 2, the highest rate
ever. Our policies are already working. Thank you.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I am astonished that the Labour
Party would initiate a snap debate on this topic this afternoon. It has to amount to one of
the greatest political own goals that I have seen in my 5 year s in this House. The reason
is very clear, but I want to restate it, part icularly for the benefit of anyone who may
have just tuned in to the debate in the last 20 minutes.
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15229
What we are talking about here is clearly a result of the failure of policy initiated and
enacted by Labour, because not one of the children whose re sults we are looking at in
this particular exercise is in any wa y caught up by the policies that the National
Government has taken in order to turn things  round. The reality is that the children who
did well under the Programme for Internati onal Student Assessment back in 2000 had
been educated under a National Government in the 1990s. Then we had 9 years of the
Clark Government, during whic h time Labour told us: “You don’t need to assess. You
do not need to monitor. You do not need to  have accurate reporting. All you need to do
is trust that all will be well.”
Well, I want to remind members of this H ouse that I was a teacher, and I am very
proud to say I was a teacher. I was a secondary school teacher, and I found that to be
one of the most rewarding and challenging thin gs I have ever done in my life. We all
know that teachers have a hugely  challenging job. It  is a dynamic, very complex, very
rewarding, and, at times, very frustrating profession. So I acknowledge the huge job that
is done by teachers the length and breadth of this country, and I am very proud to have
worked with many of them and to consider many of them my friends.
I have to say, I was not impressed by the absolute baloney and propaganda I had to
sit through last Friday night in a DVD put together by the New Zealand Educational
Institute, which was nothing but a slanderous  attack on the current Government and our
Ministers. If that was a professional thing by a group of teachers, then I have to say
thank goodness that more and more of them are turning away from the New Zealand
Educational Institute. But let us not for one moment negate the important job that
teachers are doing, and I do acknowledge them.
So why have we got to this point? Is it a lack of investment? We ll, clearly, it is not,
because successive Governments have increas ed the investment in education and this
Government, I am very proud to say, has in creased Vote Education by 40 percent since
2008. We are now investing 20 pe rcent of all public expendit ure in education, which is
the second-highest percentage of  any Government in the OECD  invest in education. So
it is not a lack of investment. Could it be the lack of a coherent and effective and
relevant curriculum? No, that is not true either, because we know that the New Zealand
curriculum is highly regarded internationally.
So it has to be something else—and it is a range of factors. There is no question
about that. We all know that many childre n are dragged into school or pushed into
school, and many of them do not get ther e. Truancy is a factor. Dysfunctional
backgrounds are a factor. We know that th ere are a whole range of socio-economic
factors that go into the mix. But what we ha ve to do is say: “We’ve got to get them
there and we are not going to accept the fact th at some of them are doomed to failure.”
And, unfortunately, that was the philosophy of the previous Government.
We are saying that one in five not achieving anything is not good enough, and we are
determined to raise the bar. I salute Anne  Tolley for the huge work she did, in the face
of some appalling opposition and personal abuse, to show, when she was the Minister of
Education, that we were serious in our comm itment to the New Z ealand public that we
would raise achievements in education. We are doing it, and the results are showing
through. In 5 to 10 years’ time, when we are having another debate in this House on the
Programme for International Student Assessmen t results, I guarantee that we will be
looking at better results.
I want to salute the Hon He kia Parata for carrying on. Sh e took the baton from Anne
Tolley after the last election, and she has continued to do a good job. I want to tell you
how incredibly proud I am to be a colleague of Hekia Parata. I have seldom seen any
Minister subjected to such appalling abuse and such misinformation as she is. Whenever
she comes to Hamilton, she makes a terrific  impression. I have hosted her at a public
15230 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
meeting. The media is not interested in covering it, but she tackles head-on all the topics
the people are interested in. She answers in a very full, coherent, and reasonable way all
the questions. And I have to say, what is mo st important is that she is absolutely
passionate about education. She speaks with the passion of one who really cares about
what she is doing. She loves the job and she is achieving what we need her to. I am
confident that we are on the right track under our polic ies, and I say shame on the
previous Government for getting us to this position.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I just wish to advise the
House—[Interruption] Order! [Interruption] Order! Order! Relax—relax. [Interruption]
Order! Order! We have members interjecting on each other and it is not permitted under
Speakers’ rulings. I call the honourable member  Jacinda Ardern and advise the House
that this is a split call.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Can I take National’s one? I am going to go for 10
minutes, Mr Assistant Speaker. If you buzz me at  5, then I will know it is split, and if it
is not, then I will sit down.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: You have got a split call
with the Mana Party.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to rectify some of the absolute rot that has
been flying around this House, not least the last call taken by someone who purported to
be a part of the education system and who claimed—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Attack me persona lly because you don’t want to deal with the
issues.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: —that there was no testing in our education system under
Labour. That is an absolutely ridiculous statement.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: I’ve talked about the issues and you attack me.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: If he was a teacher, he woul d know that I have not made a
personal attack. I have simply pointed out that if Mr Macindoe was a member of the
education system under Labour, he would know that there was testing, and there was.
My second point is that we  heard within 10 seconds of  Mr Calder’s speech and
within Mr Macindoe’s speech blatant attacks on the teachers of this country who have
taken it upon themselves to raise their con cerns about the teaching environment. That
was absolutely legitimate that they did. To be vilified as union hacks in doing so is an
absolute disgrace.
The point I want to come to is this: the e nvironment that that Government has talked
about has been solely isolated to the teach ing environment. We on this side of the
House have raised our concerns with what has happened in the last 5 years, but what
that Government refuses to acknowledge is that a child does not go to school and exist
in a bubble. In the last 5 years that these children a nd these young people have been
attending and been part of our education system, there ha ve been other things going on
in their lives that affect their educational outcomes.
The OECD acknowledges that—the OECD ac knowledges that. I want  to refer to the
section from the OECD Programme for International Student Assessment report that has
not been talked about yet. It talks about the impact of inequality on educational
outcomes. It states this: “New Zealand and Chinese Taipei are the only two high-
performing countries/economies with below- average levels of e quity in education
outcomes. Targeting low-performing and/or  disadvantaged student s is a policy option
for both of these countries, as the steepness of the gradient suggests that low-performing
students could rapidly improve their perfor mance if their socio-economic status is
improved.” Chinese Taipei and New Zealand virtually get their own graphic indication
of the fact that young people who are growi ng up with economic disadvantage are also
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15231
performing badly and that inequality is havi ng an impact on the kids who are tested in
this report.
If that Government wants to stand there and say that the last 5 years have not
mattered, it clearly has absolutely no idea a bout the reality that these kids are growing
up with. To assume that the economic environm ent of their parents and of their families
has no impact on their educational outcome is to turn a blind eye to the environment
that they are living in. If the Government n eeded any more evidence, in the equity and
outcomes section of the repor t there is also more disc ussion about disparities and
performance related to socio-economic status, where, again, New Zealand is isolated as
one of only two schooling systems where there is a complete disconnect, given the fact
that we have a well-performing economy, but children who are living in absolute
disadvantage are not performing—are not performing.
This is part of the problem. There is a lot more going on in our education system,
which has been talked about by Chris Hipkins, but for that Government to ignore that its
5 years of government has not had an impact on those children is an absolute disgrace,
because what kind of outcomes does it lead  to? Well, we know fr om the reports that
have come out of the Ministry of Social Development that material deprivation includes
lack of access to educational tools. Kids w ithout computers in homes, kids who cannot
afford to go on school trips—these are all m easured and we are failing them. Kids, for
instance, who do not have more than two pa irs of school shoes, kids who do not have
uniforms and therefore do not go  to school because they ca nnot afford them and they
are ashamed, children who do not have e nough food to take to school and sometimes
stay at home because of it as well—if this Government was serious about improving
educational outcomes, it would support Ma na’s Education (Food in Schools)
Amendment Bill. It would support that bill to  demonstrate that it is worried about the
environment that these children are growing up in, but clearly it thinks that it is all down
to the fact that teachers are part of a union and that somehow that has been the failure of
our education system. That Government n eeds to acknowledge the environment that
young people are experiencing and then, perh aps, we might see some educational
improvements.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. T ēnā
tātou katoa e te Whare, e noho tahi ana, e k ōrero tahi ana ki t ēnei kaupapa
whakahirahira kai mua i a t ātou i t ēnei r ā. Nō reira, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, kia ora
tātou katoa.
[Greetings, Mr Assistant Speaker. Greetings to us all the H ouse, seated together and
speaking together to this important matter before us today. And so I acknowledge and
greet you collectively, and thank us all.]
National’s education policies have just take n a major hammering in an international
assessment that has heavily downgraded New Zealand students’ achievements in maths,
science, and reading, yet all the Minister of Education can do is trot out some irrelevant
philosophical rubbish and tell the Opposition to stop playing the blame game. But the
ugly reality—and I have not heard people me ntion it too often and somebody needs to
say it—is that New Zealand’s educati on ranking has fallen from seventh to 18 th in
science, from 13 th to 23 rd in maths, and from seventh to 13 th in reading, according to a
report released by the Organization for Ec onomic Cooperation and Development last
night. Yet this Government point-blank refu ses to accept that the deteriorating test
scores and New Zealand dropping out of th e top 10 are because of its out-of-touch
education policies.
The Programme for International Student  Assessment—PISA—highlights the fact
that National’s approach has increased inequities between  schools. It notes that the gap
between test scores in high-decile and low-decile schools is bigger than ever before, and
15232 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
ranks this country, New Zealand, firmly in the bottom third of OECD countries in terms
of equity ratings. Yet despite all of th e Government’s hot air about lifting the
achievement of all learners and especially those in low- decile schools, it has done
precisely nothing to address the fact that  poverty and inequali ty matter hugely to
learning achievement.
Instead, this Government has done everythi ng it can to entrench and exacerbate
poverty and inequality, like cutting funding to early childhood education and State
schools while increasing funding to priv ate schools and now charter schools and
grinding down the already low incomes and living conditions of struggling wh ānau.
This Government continues to refuse to acknowledge the fact that poverty and
inequality matter at all, even though it ha s had ample evidence from experts about how
important it is to address equity issues if  it seriously wants to  address educational
underachievement. For example, we know that the Government curren tly helps to feed
children through KidsCan and KickStart Brea kfast, but we also  know that 80,000
children are still going to school hungry. All of those children are our children, and they
are going hungry. We know—because all of the facts tell us so—that hungry children of
whatever race, colour, or creed simply do not learn well. We know too that a
Government-funded food programme, as spoken of in the Programme for International
Student Assessment report, in low-deci le schools has been recommended as an
immediate way to help address child pove rty, raise educational achievement, and
improve child health by a rang e of groups and organisations right here in New Zealand
in recent years, and most recently by the Children’s Commissioner’s Expert Advisory
Group on Solutions to Child Poverty in its final report released in December last year.
We know too that my Feed the Kids bill— whether it is mine or David Shearer’s
Education (Food in Schools) Amendment Bill —aims to provide free meals to all
students in decile 1 and 2 schools,  and won broad support from groups and
organisations right across the country, including the Child Poverty Action Group, Every
Child Counts, Unicef New Zealand, Save the Children, IHC, the Methodist and
Anglican churches, Te R ōpū W āhine M āori Toko i te Ora, the New Zealand
Educational Institute, the Post Primary Teachers Association, the New Zealand
Principals’ Federation, the CTU R ūnanga, the New Zealand Nu rses Organisation, and
the M āori Medical Practiti oners Association. Yet this Government still refuses to
acknowledge the importance of equity, of nu trition, and of the need for a fully
Government-funded food in schools programme.
The Programme for International Student  Assessment report also recommended
increasing equity, increasing resources, and providing help for poor children, but this
Government has chosen to put its energy into other areas like national standards, private
education, and charter schools. The Program me for International Student Assessment
report pointed out that disadva ntaged schools struggle to at tract qualified teachers and
that poor kids suffer as a result.
It also pointed out the obvious fact that  high-performing countries—I have not heard
the bell, Mr Assistant Speaker—pay teachers well and actually choose that as a policy
priority over reducing cl ass size, and that they also put a lot of focus into ensuring that
high-performing teachers actually get placed in socially disadvantaged schools. Yet
what does this Government do? It conti nues to blame teachers and the education
system. It attacks teachers unions, criticises teachers’ standards, cuts back on curriculum
advisers, and even goes so far as to suggest that 6-year-old kids rate teachers, all the
while paying those teachers through a broke n Novopay system, the sum result of which
has been to confuse, confound, and demora lise teachers in what has been widely
recognised as one of the best te aching collectives in the world. T ēnā koutou. Kia ora
tātou katoa.
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15233

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Excuses, excuses, and more excuses.
Every time we talk about education, what do we get from Labour and its close friends
the unions? All we have heard for the last fe w years is excuses, excuses, and all the
while our students have been falling behind—s lowly, steadily, and surely falling behind
the rest of the world. It is always someone else ’s fault. It is never Labour’s fault. It is
never that Government’s fault. And when we  dared to suggest that we actually follow
and measure a child’s progress and talk to th e parents about that ch ild’s progress, what
did we get from the unions and from Labour—nothing, nothi ng helpful, nothing
constructive. They fought it actively every st ep of the way. They said to us: “We don’t
need to measure anything.”
I have heard principals stand up and ask “Why are we measuring kids’ progress,
because, actually, if they fall behind a little bit in those first years, they will catch up
when they’re ready”. I have had parents say to me that they have been told time and
time again by their teachers: “Don’t worry about  little Johnny if he’s not learning to
read yet, because he’l l catch up when he gets a bit ol der.” Well, they have not caught
up.
Now that the evidence is clear, Labour and the teache r unions should be hanging
their heads in shame, because they have failed those kids. There are no excuses. They
have to take responsibility. They sat there for 9 years as a Government and believed it
when the unions told them that everythi ng was OK. The union ma ntra was “We know
who these kids are who are failing.” And I heard Chris Hipkins say that again this
morning—“We know who these kids are who ar e failing.” Well, my question is always
“What did you do for 9 years while you watched those kids fail?”, because this
Programme for International Student Assessm ent result is telling us that you watched
them continue to fail and you did nothing. You had huge surpluses. You could have
done something and you did nothing.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: She is the guilty woman. She cut the professional
development.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: You were a Minister, Mr Mallard, and you were
responsible—after National had been in Government.
I have a quote on my whiteboard on my office.  I have kept it because to me it sums
up everything that is wrong w ith the New Zealand Educati onal Institute and the New
Zealand Principals’ Federation in this coun try. It was from a principal who was a
member of both. In a letter to me he said : “The implied message from these national
standards is that everyone in New Zealand ha s to be literate and numerate. What a sad
place school will be if this type of nonsense continues.” That is from a New Zealand
primary school principal, a leading princi pal in both the New Zealand Educational
Institute and the New Zealand Principals’ Fe deration, who does not think it is important
for kids to learn to read and write. That is why our prisons are overflowing with
prisoners who cannot read and write.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Go to Kimi Ora and say that. The Minister’s talking
nonsense.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: This member should take a call if he wants to take part in
this debate instead of casting aspersions across the House, and no one is really
interested. That is why our prisons are full of prisoners who cannot read and write. They
have not been able to hold down a job and they have no skills that would make them
employable, and that is why we are now facing the truth about our education system—
that our 15-year-olds are not the best in the world any more because, actually, when it
came down to it Labour did not care. It did no t care enough to stand up to the teacher
unions and demand change in an education system that was failing kids.
15234 Urgent Debates 4 Dec 2013
Well, on this side of the House we do care.  We have put students and their parents
first, we have stood up to  the unions, and we have in troduced a range of changes
designed to address the failure that we all knew was coming—because we did know that
this day was coming. We were warned. I we nt off to the OECD as Minister of
Education and it told me that it had warned  the previous Labour Government too that
the education system in New Zealand was getting complacent, that it was not based on
evidential learning—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That’s a lie—didn’t tell me that.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: That is not a lie. Mr Schl eicher warned the Labour
Government that it had to make systemic changes and he warned me. We were putting
in national standards and the OECD has c ontinued to back the changes that this
Government has made. But it is not going to happen overnight, and I said in 2010, when
we introduced those standards, that it coul d take 5 years or more before we saw
substantial change in our system. I said in  2010 that there had been no change in our
reading performance since 2000—that was 9 years under a Labour Government—and
no change in maths since 2003. So we should not  be surprised when we see the results
that we are facing here today.
Remember that national standards were  introduced by the Labour Government
because one in five of our kids in school was failing. In other words, the schools were
failing them. The education system was fa iling them and the Labour Government had
failed them. Education Minister after educa tion Minister did not have the courage to
stand up to the unions and make the changes they knew needed to be made. Minister
Mallard knew that there needed to be cha nges made and the union actually backed him
down. He did not go through with what he knew needed to be done.
This Government introduced the Youth Guar antee, which was designed to give free
education to students up to age 18 who ha d dropped out of the schooling environment.
They had been deserted by Labour, whose onl y answer was to lift the school-leaving
age. Well, actually, those kids were not at  school anyway. They were some of the
30,000 truants every day from our schooling sy stem. This Government tackled those
kids with some innovative programmes between secondary and tertiary institutions—
things like trades academies, service academies, and tertiary education for trades
education in tertiary institutions, and now we are seeing over 10,000 of those young
people re-engaged in education and getting sk ills and training and qualifications. These
are fantastic results for kids whom Labour abandoned.
Labour continues to back the unions over kids. We have heard it from Labour
members today. They want no change in the system. They are promising to roll back all
the changes that National has made over th e last 5 years should they ever—for the
unfortunate sake of the count ry—reach Treasury benches. So they want more of the
same as through those years of the 2000s when  kids were being failed by the education
system. Is that really what they are prom oting? Well, I welcome these Programme for
International Student Assessment results because they show that National has been right
all along. The education system did need a sy stemic change. We have been right to
shake up the education system on behalf of kids and on behalf of their parents.
I am still approached by parents in airports who say “Thank goodness you guys stood
up for us and made sure that we got good in formation about what is happening to our
children early on in their school time so that we can make sure that we support them and
we help them learn while they are in those all-important primary years.” So all I can say
to Labour is “Just get out of the way.”, beca use this side of the House is absolutely
determined, as the Minister of Education has said, to make sure that five out of five kids
succeed in our schools. We have got a lot of  work to do and we want those people out
of our way.
4 Dec 2013 Urgent Debates 15235
