items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I move, That the
House take note of miscellaneous business . This afternoon yet again we have had
another couple of revealing glimpses of the true state of the New Zealand Labour Party.
There are two particular points this afte rnoon—firstly, during question time and, I have
to say, the incredibly lazy, incredibly de luded performance of the Opposition leader,
who turned up and wasted thr ee-quarters of his side’s ques tions on a lazy attack on the
Prime Minister, which was of absolutely no substance. There was absolutely no
preparation. It had absolutely no point. And, on top of that, he was well and truly
spanked by the Prime Minister. It is not as if this was the first time. The Opposition
leader persists in coming down here with hi s airs and graces a nd pretending that he
knows stuff, and absolutely is as shallow as a puddle.
Speaking of shallow puddles, the second g limpse we got of the New Zealand Labour
Party this afternoon was its incredibly sha llow political attack on the Programme for
International Student Assessmen t results. Actually, it is qui te revealing if you have a
look at it, because Labour’s first move act ually happened yesterday when it broke an
international, 34-country embargo to score a shallow political proced ural stunt in this
House before the results were released. That has to be the most j uvenile approach to
what is a serious subject for New Zealand. Then, having made the juvenile attack,
15236 General Debate 4 Dec 2013
which was completely over the heads of most  New Zealanders, it proceeded to attack
the Government for the results. Well, let me tell you one thing. These results, if we want
to be political about it, were nurtured and created by the previous Labour Government.

items.speaker: Some maths lessons for the Opposition
items.text: 15-ye ar-olds last year were 5-year-olds in
2002 and they were 3-year-olds in 2000. They  spent their entire preschool and primary
school years in Labour’s utopian school sy stem. People in glass houses should not be
throwing stones. Mr Hipkins worked then for the uber-Minister of Education, one T
Mallard—he of the “The world is lying.” sort of accusation— and the deal is that they
were the Labour Government’s results. We  can all accept that the numbers have
declined, and that means, frankly, that we are all responsible as a country. And because
of the time it takes for educati on results to appear, everybody in this House has to have
a look at themselves because this decline is not new. It has been around for a while. So
even now, the maths decline—what were th e numbers in 2009? Thirteen. They have
declined since then. But what were they in  2000? We were at four 2000, so we declined
then. So if the cri ticism is of the National Governme nt now, then what about that
period? It is adolescen t of Mr Hipkins, I have to say, to blame the current Government.
Let us accept that there has been a decline.
So what new, innovative things are partie s proposing to actually achieve with this
stuff? Well, partnership schools—a National Party initiative. Netw ork for Learning—a
National Party initiative. Par ticipation targets in early childhood education—a National
Party initiative. The Youth Guarantee—a hi ghly successful Nationa l Party initiative.
National Certificate of Educational Achiev ement level 2 targets, performance-linked
funding in tertiary education, and national st andards in primary schools—we need more
of this innovation, not less. You cannot ma nage what you cannot measure, and the
Labour Party and the Green Party in this H ouse today using measures to criticise the
Government for having measures was ironic. That is what they were doing. They were
saying that the Programme for International Student Assessment measures are the things
that we should have to criticise the Government for measuring national standards. If that
is not hypocrisy, what is?
The sad part about it is that the Labour Party and the Green Party have no solution
except to wind everything back. That is the trouble for the Labour Pa rty, and that is the
other thing we have noticed today: the laz y, inept attack on national standards and the
fact that it has done absolutely no work on polic y in this area except to say that it would
roll it back. That says that the Labour Part y is lazy. The Labour Party, after 5 years in
Opposition, is still arrogant, because it st ill believes that it does not need any new
policies to get itself re-elected. I have one suggestion for those members. When they go
away in the break, for goodness’ sake, do some work, because your laziness is showing.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I hope my voice holds out for this debate. This
is not a bad Government. It  is not a mediocre Govern ment. This is an awful
Government. It is such a woeful Government  that it is difficult to know where to start
and where to stop. Well, a good place to star t is today. During question time today, our
leader, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, brought into the daylight just the latest in a long line
of failures. We have exposed just how une thically the Government has acted over the
defunct Learning Media. We have revealed how the Government changed the contract
rules that are sending Learning Media into ba nkruptcy, yet it is a dvancing capital to the
company to repay Westpac, a foreign-owned ba nk creditor, in full. Never mind the rest.
Never mind the others who will be left out  of pocket—elderly investors who own the
building that Learning Media resided in.
The list of this Government’s failures is a long one. The recent revelations about
falling education standards are deeply al arming to all those who have school-age
children. I certainly can recall my three children growing up in a period when we prided
4 Dec 2013 General Debate 15237
ourselves on our education system, and that continued right through, with my last child
leaving college in only the last year or so. I can recall when the school system was good
and was continuing to provide for our young one s. Under this Government we have the
cuts, the changes, the move to the likes  of charter schools, and the funding of $36
million to the likes of private schools, to th e detriment of State sc hools. It all goes on
and on. This Government has a woeful track record in terms of education.
The country has had its best te rms of trade in 40 years, but  that is not something that
this Government can take credit for. It is b ecause of our agriculture. It is because of our
dairy. It is because of our forestry, our meat, our seafood, and all our other
manufactured exports.
The housing market is in crisis. The plight  of first-home buyers is absolutely dire,
with Kiwis—good Kiwis—dreaming of homeo wnership and young ones sick to see
what is happening. Just last week I attende d an auction in my own suburb of Campbells
Bay on the North Shore, and was aghast to  see a small piece of land, less than 500
square metres, sell for over $1 million—for a bare piece of dirt. And do you know
where the buyers were from? They were  not good, honest, everyday, working Kiwis.
All the Kiwis got knocked out at around the $800,000 mark and it was sold to people
from abroad. We do not even know whether those people from abroad had New Zealand
residency.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: That’s racist.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: No, it is not racist. It is what is happening, Mr Coleman,
all over Auckland at the present time. New Zeal and First stands for putting in place that
you must be a New Zealand resident and you mu st be domiciled here in this country to
purchase here. You cannot sit back in some foreign country—whether it be in Europe,
whether it be in the United States, whether it be in Asia—and buy land from under the
noses of good, hard-working Kiwis.
Immigration is out of cont rol. It is a total shambl es, with young New Zealanders
having to contend with tens of  thousands of immigrants in a very weak market for jobs.
For the people of Christchurch, they must  endure a stumbling, bumbling recovery of
their city. The Government has taken a bit of a bath this last weekend in Christchurch
East, where people are still in dire straits. The Government has plans to rejuvenate the
central business district, pull down perf ectly good public libra ries, and pull down
perfectly good other buildings so that it  can build its convention centre down in
Christchurch while people in the eastern suburbs are still suffering.
Let us remember some of the many other fiascos this Government has brought
about—the likes of South Canterbury Fina nce. It was allowed a blowout of $800
million and 6 months went by while the Government turned a blind eye as more
investments were being made in South Cant erbury Finance. The Government gave $30
million to Rio Tinto without making sure there was an assurance of job security for the
future for the people of Sout hland. The Government was re sponsible for the absolute
abomination that is Novopay, and it allowed that hideous situation to continue where
teachers in this country are still suffering from disruption to their pay cycles. The
Government gave Warner Bros $67 million fo r a movie that grossed over $1 billion
worldwide, when a loan would have seen the taxpayers’ advance secured.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I want to address the
reforms, the way we are working with young people, and the difference that we are
making in their lives. We have heard a lo t of rubbish from the Opposition today about
how we have seen the demise of young pe ople, how dreadfully they are all doing, and
how it is everyone’s fault, of  course, except theirs—and mainly ours. Well, I want to
stand up here today and say that I actually think young people are thriving and doing
incredibly well. They have an awesome futu re, and the ones whom I meet, if our hands
15238 General Debate 4 Dec 2013
are in theirs, I think we are goi ng to be pretty much all righ t. There are some things we
can do better, and you have alrea dy heard from previous speake rs from this side of the
House on where that attention is going, wh ere the resources are at, and how we are
targeting more to those who need it most. I stand here, certainly, myself, and I am proud
of the fact that we get the right informati on on the right people so that we are able to
make sure the right resources are getting to them.
If ever there is an example of where that is happening the most, it would have to be
in youth services within our welfare reform s, particularly for those young people aged
16, 17, and 18. Let us cut to the facts of what  we did not know before but we do know
now. Of those aged 30 to 39 years old who ar e currently on a benef it, 60 percent went
on as a teenager—of those currently aged 30 to 39 who are on a benefit, 60 percent went
on as a teenager. Of young beneficiaries, 43 pe rcent will still be on  a benefit 15 years
later. Of disengaged 16 and 17-year-olds, 90 percent will go on an adult benefit at age
18 or 19 unless we intervene differently.
So, of course, that is exactly what we did. We went out there. We contracted. We got
all that new money in the Budget of 2012. We then implemented our youth services and
we see substantial differences for these young people. Of thos e who were not in
education, employment, or training—so those who were “neets”—we now have 59
percent enrolled in education, another 17 percent in training, and another 4 percent in
work-based learning. That is outstanding. We have 1,300 who are on the new youth
payment, which are those 16 and 17-year-o lds. Of those 1,300, 71 percent are in
education—71 percent. I can tell you that th at number was pretty much zero before
these reforms came in. But—and it will not surprise many in this House—the ones who
really get me going the most, and who, I th ink, are making the bigge st difference, are
those teen parents. Of teen parents ag ed 16, 17, and 18 years old, we have got 1,400
who are on a young parent payment. Of them, 70 percent are in education, 13 percent
are in training, 48 percent have done a budgeting course, and 44 percent have done a
parenting course.
But there is a reason I got into politics and I have been reminded of it this week. I get
to indulge myself in the general debate, whic h is a pleasure we do not often get in this
House. I am thrilled to say that I ha d a young woman who wrote to me and said:
“Because I was now single with no income, I had to apply for a solo benefit. I went to
Youth Service to sign up for the youth benefit. I had absolutely no levels from school as
I had dropped out so young at 14. Basically, I ha d nothing to offer my girl. When I met
the Youth Service officer, they made me go into education, and told me I wouldn’t get a
benefit unless I was enrolled in some type of course.”

items.speaker: She then goes on further. She says
items.text: “They were all absolutely welcoming to me, and
absolutely loving and caring. I had to break the habit of staying home all day long to
actually get up early and do something with my self for the day. After the first term was
over and the second term started, I was still not attending regularly, so my teacher spoke
to me and told me I had to attend at least part  time if I wanted to keep getting paid my
youth service benefit. That was when my lif e practically changed.  I didn’t want to
struggle with a baby so I carried on at TPU,  the teen parent unit. The second term at
TPU was the best time I had in a long time. I finally felt like I belonged somewhere.
School was always hard for me to attend, but now I am achieving.”
I had another one who wrote to me and said: “Before I started at the TPU and was
made to go, I only had level 1 Achieved. I didn’t actually real ise I had any NCEA
credits. But now since the teen parent’s coming to an end, with only 6 weeks left, I have
level 1, 2, and 3, and only need 11 more credits to complete university entrance.” I have
another young woman here who told me that the reality for her wa s: “I have gained
level 2 while I have been he re, and am 10 credits away fr om completing level 3. I have
4 Dec 2013 General Debate 15239
also put credits towards university entrance. The TPU and the girls here have motivated
me so much to make a better change for myself.”
That is why we come into Parliament—to change these girls’ lives, to see them get
educational achievement, and to see them gr ow into who we know they can be. This
side of the House backs them.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: There is absolutely no doubt that despite the odd
positive anecdotal story from a Minister —we could probably count them on our
hands—this is absolutely a Government in d ecline. It is difficult for me to narrow down
for a 5-minute speech the various ways in which we can see that this is a Government in
decline. Probably the biggest demonstration of that, the best exam ple I could come up
with, is that in order to return to Budget su rplus, this is a Government that could do
nothing else but sell all our stuff—sell all our stuff.
The first thing that the Government could do, the best option it came up with when it
wanted to make sure we got out of the red, wa s to sell our assets. That is absolutely a
relevant issue for us to continue to debate t oday. This is a Governme nt that is arrogant
enough to absolutely ignore the views of Ne w Zealanders. It has dismissed, from the
beginning, poll after poll that has demonstrat ed that it was a completely unpopular
policy, to the point that the Prime Minister  has arrogantly claimed time and time again
that simply by voting for National, everyone said they were happy with assets being
sold. That is absolutely untrue. More people voted for parties that did not agree with
asset sales than for those that did.
So the message that needs to go out clearly in the midst of this referendum is that this
is a Prime Minister who will interpret every vote that is not cast as simply someone
saying that they love his wor k. So everyone must exercise th eir democratic right if they
would rather not have the Prime Minister sk ew their view. We w ill continue to do our
job by ensuring that this Government listens to the voices of New Zealanders who time
and time again have expressed their anger over these asset sales.
But I would also ask that people cast their vote on behalf of those who are unable to
have their say—those who are not eligible to cast a vote  but who are the generation
from whom we continue to strip everythi ng away. They are a generation that is
suffering in the wake of a Government in decline. They are the No Generation. We have
heard every other label for a generation that is possible: Generation Y, the Millennials,
and the C Generation. This is the No Gene ration: no house, no free education, and
potentially no superannuation, given the way this Government has no plan to ensure that
their future retirement is secure. This is a group of young people who are suffering
because this is a Government th at has absolutely lacked vision for what it is that they
will need in the future.
There are 78,000 members of this No Ge neration who are currently not in
employment, not in education, and not in trai ning. They are the next cohort of 15-year-
olds who will be measured by the Program me for Internationa l Student Assessment
report, and they are failing. We had Anne To lley say: “It is their fault”. We had Hekia

items.speaker: Parata say
items.text: “It is not my fault”. We had Stev en Joyce say: “It is everyone’s fault”. At
the end of the day, Labour has not been in Government for 5 years. The buck has to stop
somewhere—the buck has to stop somewher e. These young people have been walking
through a school gate to a school where teac hers have been stripped of professional
development, have had every change unde r the sun bearing down on them, and have
been attacked by this Government. A nd these young people themselves have
experienced deprivation that has negatively impacted upon them.
There are 270,000 children growing up in poverty in this country. Ms Bennett may
stand up here and tell us about all the teen agers who are doing well. I agree that there
are some who are doing phenomenally well , who are wonderful young people, and we
15240 General Debate 4 Dec 2013
should be proud of every single one of them. But there is a cohort that is not doing well,
and we cannot ignore that fact. The Youth’12 survey told us th at 29 percent of young
women in our high schools are self-har ming—29 percent—and 21 percent have
seriously considered suicide in the past year . It is no wonder that  in this OECD report
we come 39th in terms of students’ happiness at school.
That side of the House may dismiss that as  not being a measure that is included in
something like national standards, bu t an unhappy young person does not succeed. A
young person who is depressed does not succeed. One in five of our students in our
schools is experiencing mental h ealth issues. One in five st udents is also being cyber-
bullied—all of these things are connected. Th is is a generation that is suffering under
the weight of a Government in decline.
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister for Communications and Information
Technology): Today we have been discussing e ducation in some detail, and it is a
critical topic. It is a topic that is fundamental to the success of our country. What we
have seen overnight from the Programme fo r International Student Assessment, out of
the OECD, is that the decline in our educ ational standards that began in 2000 is
continuing. That is a matter that I know is of  concern to the entire House, because if our
people are not coming through schools with the skills that they need to build a future for
themselves, we all need to be worried about that.
This is not a simple issue. It is an issue that requires a multi-pronged approach to its
solution. That is something that this Govern ment recognised from the day that it took
office, and it has been delivering real changes to the way that we educate our children to
turn that round. Every single time that this Government has had a plan to do something
tangible about that, Labour has opposed it. La bour has opposed it because it is far more
interested in protecting its union mates than it is worried about the children.
This is the Government that brought in national standards. We want to know whether
our children are succeeding. We need to know this in primary school, not once they get
to high school, and then think: “Gosh, why are we not getting there?”. In fact, the
children that this Programme for Interna tional Student Assessment surveyed went
through those critical primary school years und er the Labour system of education. Now
we have national standards that will help us  to identify and address those shortcomings
considerably more.
We are investing a huge amount in the qual ity of our teachers be cause we know that
the one thing that will make  a difference, more than an ything else, is high-quality
teachers. We want to support that. But it is also about providing the resources to our
schools to raise educational standards and to make sure that every child in every school
has access to the resources that they would have in the best schools. A big part of that is
through digital enablement.
I want to commend my collea gue the Hon Nikki Kaye, w ho is leading a programme
of work through the Network for Learning. Th is programme is taking advantage of the
ultra-fast broadband that National is rolling out to schools, because we know that that
sort of digital connect ivity is absolutely cr itical in preparing ch ildren for the modern
world. The ultra-fast broadband has so far been rolled out to more than 1,900 schools.
By 2016 every school in this country will ha ve access to ultra-fast broadband and will
have access to the Network for Learning. That means that every child in every school,
from the smallest to the larges t, will be able to access the best resources offered in the
best schools in the world. Is that not interesting?
The Labour Opposition has done everything it can for 5 years to derail ultra-fast
broadband. It voted against it. It tried to block it. It complained that it was all happening
too fast; it complained that it was a ll happening too slow. We are now seeing the
Opposition getting behind a campaign to try once more to derail it. Why is it doing that?
4 Dec 2013 General Debate 15241
It is doing that for its own selfish, politic al, short-focused, shor t-sighted, self-serving
gains. That is the only reason it is doing it.
Do you know who benefits from this ? Do you know who would benefit from
derailing the build of ultra-fast broadband? I can tell you who it is not benefiting. It is
not the consumers; it is the retailers. So if we insist on a lower price for the wholesalers,
as Labour wants to happen—follow the money. Follow the money. I will tell you who
benefits: the large corporates like Vodafone , which benefits from the extra money. That
is what Labour is supporting. That is what it wants to see happen.
I will tell you what will happen now. The consumers will not see anything at all, I
predict. If they do, it will be a tiny fr action of any drop. Do you know why? Because
now we are going to be embroiled in years and years of litigation while the retailers
fight very hard to keep thos e profits. If anybody in this House is naive enough to think
that this is about consumers,  they are dreaming. This fight is about making the retailers
keep the extra money. It is the big corporate retailers that we are seeing Labour get in
behind. The retailers are now coming out and sa ying: “Oh, well, we don’t think we will
be able to pass any of it on. Sorry about that. Oops!”. Well, that is exactly what we have
been saying.
I would suggest to the opponents in this House who are trying so hard to derail ultra-
fast broadband—who are trying so hard to stop New Zealand schools, New Zealand
families, getting access to world-leading e ducation and world-leading health services—
that the economic benefits al one of ultra-fast broadband ar e massive. It is creating so
many jobs around New Zealand. It has been independently modelled to add about $33
billion worth of economic benefits. Labour and the Greens are once more saying: “Let’s
just block it. Let’s stop it. Let’s say no. We are more inte rested in ourselves and our
own point-scoring than in th e people of New Zealand.” We  are not going to let that
happen.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : This Government
is failing. This is a shambolic Government that is a disgrace to democracy. I received an
email today, and so did most MPs, saying:  “Please remember those who died for
democracy, died for the freedom to vote, died  so that people could be heard. Please do
not dismiss the result of any referendum as  though it is a pain in your side or with
remarks akin to ‘It won’t change anything.’, b ecause it is a slap in the face to all those
who have served and currently serve in the armed forces; those who have committed
their lives to the protection of  our rights.” That is from a third-generation armed forces
member. All those people whom we acknowle dge on Anzac Day would be rolling over
in their graves if they knew what is going on in this country today.
Thirty pieces of silver, $30 million to Ri o Tinto, and 30 percent of the population, at
best, support asset sales—what is the common  thread there? Well, it is, in one word,
“treachery”—treachery. I went to Wikipedia—as  we all do today, of course; to the font
of all wisdom—to ask what the definition of “treason” is. It said: “citizen’s actions to …
seriously injure …” the nation. I put it to you that that is exactly what this National
Government is carrying out by ignoring the vi ews of New Zealanders . It is treachery
that is seriously undermining our ability to move forward as a country.
This Government is failing in many ar eas. Today we heard about education. The
balance of payments deficit—oh, terms of trade are good; the balance of payments
deficit is disastrous. Well, I look at a coupl e of areas of the economy, and at primary
industries in particular.
Let us look at forestry. Ther e are record export earnings in forestry—well, so we are
told. There are certainly record  log exports. So what we have seen is a record to $4.3
billion, which I think is about the fourth-biggest export from this country. The majority
of it is now going out in logs. It is $120 fo r a tonne of logs and $400 for a tonne of
15242 General Debate 4 Dec 2013
timber. The National Government is exporting jobs from this country every single day
from the forestry industry. And do you know what we are left with? We are left with an
industry under huge commercial pressure—finan cial pressure—to the point where it is
killing people in the forests on a regular basi s because of the financial pressure put on
contracting firms to rip down those logs and ge t rid of them as quickly as possible. That
is the failure of the National Government in the forestry industry.
Let us look at meat—the once-proud m eat industry. National is the party that
champions the rights of farmers. What is happening in the meat industry? Farmers are
leaving to go dairying. Even in the area of dairying we are seeing unhidden
environmental and financial costs. Let us  go back to meat—the wonderful progress—
because the National Government has committe d half a million dollars to the Red Meat
Sector Strategy, and then committed $350 m illion of taxpayer and farmer money
through the Primary Growth Partnership to  grow the red meat  industry. And do you
know what the latest innovation is? It is to take the carcasse s, cut them into six pieces,
and send them to China for further value-a dded processing. This National Government
is a disgrace to the agricultural sector . The farmers and the meatworkers who have
worked hard to build value in the meat industry have seen it destroyed in 1 single year.
Look at manufacturing. National has failed in manufacturing. At best, it has been
flat—exports of manufactured products—mainly off the back of the primary sector
because of the dairy industry.
Take away the dairy sector influence, a nd in every measure of our economy, this
National Government has failed. It is, indeed , carrying out treacher ous acts of selling
our assets and failing to build up any additional value in this economy. This
Government is a disgrace.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, I am astonished, as is everybody who
has just heard that last speech by the Hon Damien O’Connor. It was not a speech; it was
a rant. It was a rant. There were some parts of it that were so funny, it was not true. Did
I hear it right? People are going out of farming into dairying.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Out of meat farming.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Oh, out of meat farming in to dairying, as if suddenly
farming is coming to a complete halt. Is that a future Minister of agriculture? I do not
think so—I do not think so. I was shocked a nd I was also aghast when that member
suggested that the Government has killed people in forestr y. That is an appalling thing
to say, and that member should be deeply, deeply ashamed. He plays fast and loose with
personal tragedies, and I have seen it from hi m before. I did not accep t it then and I do
not now.
We are engaged in the general debate. Unlik e the previous speaker, I intend to talk
about the place I live in, and that is the West Coast and Tasman. It is one of those
splendid areas where people are worth their wei ght in gold. It is one of those areas that
is a truly revenue-generating area, and what a wonderful place it is.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: And they tossed the member out.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Say again?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: And they tossed the member out.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Not particularly. I do not think that was—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Who won the party vote?

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, who won the party vote ? We have consistently won
the party vote since I have been standing. I held the seat, and, indeed, there was a
change. But stand by, Mr Mallard , for the seat to be return ed to National, and National
will be back on the Treasury benches. Nothing is more certain than that.
Tasman and the West Coast supports dairyi ng, fishing, mining, horticulture, forestry,
and tourism. Think of that. Think of those as pects. I will say it ag ain: dairying, fishing,
4 Dec 2013 General Debate 15243
mining, horticulture, forestry, and tourism. Th ey are basic, real industries in New
Zealand. It is an area that has frequently been ravaged by Labour—ravaged and savaged
and neglected, just as that member neglec ted to mention it during his 5 minutes of
ghastly ranting. But, especia lly, that area was ravaged by th e cruel policie s of the Hon
Trevor Mallard when he was the Minister  of Education, and the school doors slammed
as he walked through the West Coast—slammed. Indeed, he was vilified—vilified.
We have had a very busy month down there. We have had Tony Ryall in Tasman,
opening the Golden Bay Integrated Family Hea lth Centre. Just compare that with what
Labour ever did in health in West Coast - Tasman. It was zilch—absolutely zilch. You
will not be hearing much from Labour about health in the next election. The Hon Tony
Ryall has dedicated $60 million to the Grey Base Hospital rebuild. What a legacy—
what a legacy. It was a pleasure to host Ma ggie Barry in the electorate for a weekend
during the last month. Her easy and natural speaking style was greatly appreciated by all
who heard her. She is an inspiration to all. The Hon Chris Tremain, the Associate
Minister of Tourism, joined an Olympic gold medallist cyclist to open the West Coast
Wilderness Trail in Kūmara a couple of weekends ago. It was a classic example of small
community recovery through a splendid policy of developm ent—a policy of the Prime
Minister’s, in fact.
We had Simon Bridges, who came dow n to open the Amethyst Hydro Scheme
electricity generation point. It was possibl e because National allows line companies to
go into generation. An extremely good day was held there, after which we took him to
visit a goldmine—a true, working goldmine—as the Minister of Energy and Resources.
It was an insightful day.
Picture if you will—picture if you will—the sort of description I have given for West
Coast - Tasman. Picture that under a Labour-G reen mixture, with perhaps New Zealand
First hanging around on the fringes. Would we  have the development? Would we have
the revenue earnings? Or would the Coast cons istently be closed? I think it would be
closed. I think, and the people of the West Co ast think—and let us remember that they
did come down and they did have a Forest an d Bird meeting. It di d not generate much
enthusiasm for anybody—no. It was sad. It was sa d, and it will be a sa d day if we have
a Labour-Green Government down on the West Coast. Thank you.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: It is a pleasure to follow the Shakespearean
tones of the National MP Chris Auchinvole. He painted a very evocative picture of a
post-apocalyptic world where the West Coas t is closed. However, the boom and bust
cycles that are attached to the industry th at he was describing—the mining industry—is
one of the reasons for those apocalyptic mome nts in the history of  areas like the West
Coast and Waihī.
However, I am not going to talk about tha t; I am going to talk about the education
system, which has been the theme this afternoon, and wh ether it is working. Even
before the Programme for International St udent Assessment survey, one might worry
when you get people who are aspiring to be leaders of political parties in Parliament
who are not sure whether man landed on the moon or are not sure whether chemtrails
are real or not. It does make us wonder wh ether the education system is not working, or
whether those are just the ramblings of an in dividual who has lost touch with reality for
some other reasons. However, it is very important—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: So do you think chemtrails are real?

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: The Green position on chemtrails is that many
people have too much time on their hands for conspiracy theories.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: No, do you believe in them or not?

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: I absolutely do not believe in chemtrails.
15244 General Debate 4 Dec 2013
In the urgent debate that we just held on education, however, the Minister of
Education told the Opposition that we shoul d stop being binary and we should have a
constructive educational convers ation. Then she yelled at the Opposition to grow up.
Unfortunately for the Minist er, this is a failed educ ational method for inspiring
dialogue, let alone change. Just agreeing with the Minister is not dialogue. Being yelled
at does not work.
I do agree with the Minister that we need to strengthen the teaching profession and
we need to support all children in Aotearoa to get the best, but wh at the Programme for
International Student Assessment survey tells us is that the bad e ducational policies of
the last 5 years in particular have entrenched  disadvantage. We need  to really look at
that survey, but it is not the be-all and end-al l. What it is telling us this time, in the
chapter on economic disadvantage and educationa l equity issues, is that our country is
decreasing when everyone else is increasi ng. Our country is failing when everyone else
is succeeding.
It is no good to just keep  trotting out these programme s for success without looking
at the context that we are operating in. The education system does not exist in a
vacuum. It is very much part of the econom ic situation of our country, which right now
is bedevilled with a number of Government  policies that are not working. Education is
just one of them. There is also the asset sales debacle, and I would urge everybody out
there to vote to make sure that the Govern ment gets the message about that very, very
clearly—that we do not want to sell our asse ts. Also there is the debacle over Skycity,
youth rates, the gutting of th e Resource Management Act, and even one of the most
mean-spirited things, which is the cup of tea.  No one is allowed a cup of tea at work.
They do not have the right to a break. That one , to me, is one of the most mean-spirited,
pathetic, and ghastly things that you would possibly imagine you could say to people in
the workplace who do not have a lot of power. After spending the night with the
cleaners in this very, very hot building, boy, did we want a cup of tea.
However, going back to the survey, if the Minister is serious about listening to it,
then she needs to adopt a Green programme of positive solutions, such as a living wage
for the parents—there is a thought. If th e survey tells us that socio-economic
disadvantage is critical, one  of the ways we help ch ildren to get socio-economic
advantage is to pay their parents enough mone y to be able to provide them with the
necessaries of life. Then all the programmes about food in schools, and all the charitable
good works that in the end do not empower people but are necessary for survival at the
moment, will not be needed because people will be earning a living wage. Another
brilliant idea would be to extend the family  in-work tax credit to all families so that
everybody would have enough to feed those children. There is an idea.
We really need to be seri ous about addressing what the survey has identified. As I
said earlier, the survey is not the endgame for education, an d some of the countries that
have been ranked really high—the Asian count ries—have authoritarian models that are
not the best models for our educational su ccess. They do not re sult in innovation,
critical thinking, and creativity, which are needed in the world today, as opposed to the
world of yesterday. Those c ountries, although ranking highly in the survey, are starting
to acknowledge that models su ch as the creative, broad cu rriculum that New Zealand
was once famous for are the kinds of models that we need.
I think that one of the most vital messages of the survey is early childhood education,
and that is where we are missing out. We  have cut the 100 percent registration
requirement, and what we are doing to P acific heritage languages, through the
Education and Science Committee, is a disgrace . It is the opposite of the survey, and it
is very disappointing.
4 Dec 2013 General Debate 15245

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: About 18 months ago I started to take a
much closer interest in education. It was not an area I had been involved in before and it
was not an area that I had taken a huge amount  of interest in. But 18 months ago my
wife and I had a child, and once you have a ch ild you start to take a much closer look at
the education system. I have to say that af ter looking at the policies that the Hon Anne
Tolley and the Hon Hekia Parata have been  putting in place for the children of New
Zealand, I have great confidence in the educ ation system that my son will be going
through. He has started in early childhood education, and in a few years’ time he will be
entering school.
We have discussed quite a bit today th e Programme for International Student
Assessment results, and it is fair to say that New Zealand has seen some decline in those
results. But I have to say I have been ab solutely appalled by some of the comments
levelled from the Opposition at the Nationa l Government’s nati onal standards policy.
Let us just remember that in 2012 the ch ildren who were assessed under the Programme
for International Student Assessment syst em were 15. They did not go through an
education system with national standards in place. It is actually the people who were
involved in that system who ar e saying that a national standa rds - type system in their
early years would have helped those children.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: When we were coming seventh, they didn’t go through it either.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Opposition members can yell and scream at us across the House,
as they have been doing all day, but the bo ttom line is that the children assessed under
the Programme for International Student Asse ssment system, which has seen the results
for this country drop, were the kids who cam e under an earlier system through primary

But the important thing is that we are working to increase the level of achievement
for all New Zealand kids. I am proud that in our country we have just doubled the

children. We have got the national standards system, the exact system that the
Programme for International Student Assessm ent people are saying will help those

like Jacinda, actually. We sat in the Television New Zealand green room most Thursday

This country is experiencing 2.5 percent growth  at the moment. It is one of the fastest
growth rates in the OECD. Tell the people who own businesses in the greater east
Tāmaki industrial area in my electorate that we are not doing bette r as a country. They
will absolutely disagree with you. Tell those em ployers that the 90-day trial, which has
led to 13,000 extra people being employed, is a bad thing. They will tell you that it is an
opportunity for them to take on new people a nd give them an opportunity. Go and talk
to the principals and the teachers in sc hools like Baverstock Oaks School in my
electorate and tell them that the policies in the education area that we are putting in

15246 General Debate 4 Dec 2013
Talk to the people who commute from Botany to the city and tell them that the

items.text: I was very interested in the comments

SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): Well, that was all rather jejune really.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: I rise as the proud member of

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: That is right—what strategy? When I first came into this

items.speaker: Ikaroa-Rāwhiti is home to many iwi

No amount of spin and no amount of make-be lieve from that side of the House will

Let us turn to youth unemployment, something that I am very passionate about.
According to the household labour force st atistics in September 2013, since National

came into office, the overall number of unemployed 20 to 24-year-olds has increased by

You can ask what Labour will do when it  comes into Government in 2014. Labour

Consideration of Interim Report of Privileges Committee
Question of Privilege Regarding Use of Intrusive Powers Within the Parliamentary
Precinct

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I move, That the House
take note of the interim report of the Privileges Committee on a question of privilege
regarding the use of intr usive powers within the parliamentary precincts.  This year the
Privileges Committee has looked at a number of  important issues. The last report that
we debated in this House related to the mu tual respect that is required to be shown
between Parliament and the courts. This re port, which has been the subject of some
work on the part of the committee since July 2013, looks at the tensions that can arise in
the parliamentary precincts between the powers and the privileges of Parliament and the
executive branch of Government. In particular, it deals with issues arising from the fact
that the Parliamentary Servic e is responsible for holding an d administering information
relating to the executive.
I want to begin by expressing my thanks to all those who gave evidence and assisted
the committee, particularly the Deputy Clerk of the House for her invaluable assistance.
Let me begin by explaining what the report was about. A question arose about the use of
intrusive powers in the parliamentary precincts, so the Speaker asked the committee to
inquire into the exercise of those intrusiv e powers against members of Parliament and,
in particular, the release of information fr om parliamentary information and security
systems.
In his reference to the Privileges Committee the Speaker set out some basic
principles. As he said, “The exercise of intrusive powers … threatens members’
freedom to carry out their functions as elec ted representatives and the House’s power to
control its own proceedings and precincts, wi thout outside interference.” So it is a very,
very important question that came to the committee.
The committee was also asked to look at th e release by the Parliamentary Service of
information that it held con cerning a journalist, including phone, email, and swipe card
access records. It is a statement of the obvious  that the media is not one of the three
branches of Government, but th ey have long been regarded as the fourth estate because
of the hugely important role that they play in informing the public about the actions of
their elected representatives.
Contrary to what some people may conte nd, this inquiry was not about trying to
relitigate the findings of the Henry investigatio n as to who leaked the Kitteridge report,
nor was it about investigating a contempt of Parliament or assigning guilt or culpability
to individuals. Its purpose was to establis h the facts of how cer tain information was
released by the Parliamentary Service, and to use those findings to inform the next step
of establishing guidelines to protect the ability  of members, as well as all those who use
the parliamentary precincts—and I refer here particularly to the fourth estate. Those
4 Dec 2013 Privilege 15251
guidelines will be the subject of the next stag e of our work, and we hope that it will be
finalised early next year.
So it was not an inquiry into  unlawfulness and the disclosure of the information. The
question does not arise, because the Privacy Act and the Official Information Act do not
apply. This in fact contributed, in my opini on, to the lack of firm principles to be
applied by the Parliamentary Service in disc losure of information. Hopefully, in the
next report, we will be addressing precisely that point.
Evidence was called from a number of people,  including representatives of the press
gallery and others involved in seeking a nd disclosing the information held by the
Parliamentary Service. At the end of the day, I think it is fair to say that most of the
background facts were probably relatively uncontested.
The Henry inquiry was issued terms of re ference by the heads of the Government
Communications Security Bureau and the Department of the Prime Minister and
Cabinet. It sought the information initially pr ovided for in the terms of reference. The
inquiry obtained the correct auth orisation to access informati on of ministerial staff held
by the Parliamentary Service on behalf of Ministerial Services. The General Manager of
the Parliamentary Service was also satisf ied that Ministers had—pre-emptively, at
least—given their consent for the information described in the terms of reference to be
released. However, he held back, or demu rred, when the inquiry sought further email
content not covered by the terms of reference, and I think this is where things started to
go wrong.
An MP who was also a Minister had emails  released by the Parliamentary Service to
the inquiry without his permission. That me mber was asked for access to his swipe card
records for, he said, a single day, but extra records were then produced. Very seriously,
a journalist’s swipe card access records were handed over wit hout her knowledge, on
the basis, the Parliamentary Service said, of  a potential security breach, when such a
breach had not been alleged by the inquiry in its request. The journalist’s full phone
records, which had been generated purely in cidentally by the Parliamentary Service,
were handed over. That was an error.
In the report, we conclude that the Henry inquiry frequently acted in what could be
called an over-vigorous manner. In turn, the Parliamentary Service failed to put in place
procedures to deal with these issues. Both ag encies failed to invol ve the Speaker, who,
as the Minister responsible for the Parliame ntary Service, could have approached these
somewhat novel and perhaps difficult questions with the correct constitutional weight.
One issue that was identified was that the Parliamentary Service, for historical
reasons, administers information systems and security matters for the entire
parliamentary precincts. Obviously, those in the precincts include not only members of
Parliament and their staff but  Ministers, media, employees of various agencies, and
contractors, many of whom are not covered by parliamentary privilege.
The former General Manager of the Parliame ntary Service told us  that his general
principle was that information belonged to me mbers and that, in general, they had the
right to control access to their particular information. This prin ciple may be a good
starting-point, but it does not catch the numerous complex situations when the
Parliamentary Service is holding information th at does not relate solely to members of
Parliament, including the facts that we were inquiring into here.
Two matters flow from these findings. The committee did not seek to, and obviously
cannot, dictate how the executive is organised. The principles of parliamentary privilege
have little to say about the responsibilities a Minister owes to Cabinet and to the Prime
Minister, at whose pleasure he or she se rves. Those are questi ons, obviously, for the
executive and not for a parliamentary committee.
15252 Privilege 4 Dec 2013
The second important point is that the res ponsibility for running Parliament’s affairs
ultimately resides with Parliament. In the evidence we heard about requests from the
inquiry for information, we heard that the i nquiry received information that it was not
entitled to.
Although this is a disappointi ng set of events, ultimately we need to work out where
we are going to go to from here. As I said, there is going to be the second report, which
picks up on the interim findings, and, hopefully, we will be able to come up with a set
of principles that will assist those dealing not only with members of Parliament but with
media and the other people who work in th ese precincts. Importa ntly, Parliamentary
Service is the administrative gatekeeper to  information held on behalf of MPs. Mr
Thorn told us that this was his basic principle, that mate rial held on behalf of MPs
would be disclosed only to those members.
There is a lot of work requi red to be done before the committee can issue its second
report. It hopes, as I said, to finalise the report early next year. I cannot speak for the
committee, but I think some clarification legisl ation is going to be required. Perhaps the
time has come to consolidate all the relevant legislation in an Act of Parliament that will
deal with the Parliamentary Service and parliamentary privilege. We have dealt recently
with the remuneration of MPs. There is legisl ation dealing with the Clerk of the House,
the Officers of Parliament, and so on. I thi nk that people are entitled to find the law
relating to this branch of Government in one statute rather than scattered throughout the
statute book, as it is at the moment. Perhaps the time has come also to take a fresh look
at the Constitution Act, which is structurally incoherent and a poor piece of legislation.
Those are the sorts of issues that we will need to look at. We will not dwell on
culpability. That was not the purpose of the inquiry; it was to find out what went wrong,
with a view to fixing things up in the future.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise
and speak on this interim report from th e Privileges Committee. I would certainly
accept one thing that the Attorney-General sa id in introducing his comments, which is
that there were a number of very serious  issues that arose during the Privileges
Committee inquiry into these matters. It is impo rtant to note that th is interim report is
about establishing what happened in this part icular incident, what  we can learn about
went wrong, and what changes are needed. This part of the inquiry is very much
grounded in what happened, and what happene d was a sorry tale of  an inquiry that,
quite frankly, was a shambles from day one.
On day one the terms of reference for th e inquiry were set, and that was done by
John Key in accordance with Wayne Eagleson, Andrew Kibblewhite from the
Department of the Prime Minister and Cabine t, and Ian Fletcher from the Government
Communications Security Bureau. They were  the people responsible for the setting of
the terms of reference. We were told at the Privileges Committee that it was John Key,
as Prime Minister, who signed off on the terms of  reference. So let us set that right at
the start—this was John Key’s inquiry, and those terms of re ference were set in such a
way that it was nearly impossible to find out  who actually leaked the Kitteridge report,
because the powers of that inquiry were set in such a way that Mr Henry was prevented
from having people appear on oath or from  having any kind of subpoenaing situation.
Inevitably, given the small range of peopl e who actually had acce ss to the Kitteridge
report, he was going to run into trouble.
So the question was raised during the Privileges Committee hearings as to whether or
not the terms of reference were set up to really find out who leaked the Kitteridge
report. As at today, although we have somebody who is acknowledged by everybody
from the Prime Minister down as the ch ief suspect—Peter D unne—we do not actually
know who leaked the Kitteridge report. The Henry inquiry was set up in such a way that
4 Dec 2013 Privilege 15253
that was almost inevitably going to be the outcome—beyond a st ark confession from
somebody in the process.
Peter Dunne today is an MP and not a Mini ster, but John Key has told us that it is
quite possible he will return as a Minister. If John Key is comfortable with Peter Dunne
returning as a Minister, then he is implicit ly saying that Peter Dunne did not leak the
report. That has to be the conclusion, and that means that this whole process—the
Kitteridge report, the Henry inquiry—has left  us none the wiser as to who leaked a
sensitive confidential document. It is, fra nkly, slack leadership by the Prime Minister
and wilful blindness as to what was actually going on in this case.
So the facts established in this inquiry were  that all of Mr Henry’s attention went to
Peter Dunne, and yet the Prime Minister is pr epared to say today that maybe he will
come back into Cabinet. I find that an unbe lievable situation and, quite clearly, the
terms of reference, I believe, were set up in such a way that they were never going to get
to the bottom of who actually leaked this report.
The major issue that came out from th e Privileges Committee investigation was
around the blurring of the lines between  the executive and Parliament. The
Parliamentary Service Act actually says in se ction 6 that Parliamentary Service is not
“an instrument of the executive government.” That is quite an unusual thing to find in
an Act—a negative statement about what Pa rliamentary Service is not—but that is
because Parliamentary Service was set up very deliberately so as not to be able to be
encumbered by the executive. What we saw throughout the process of  this inquiry was
the blurring of those lines.
The blurring of those lines occurred once Parliamentary Service agreed to release
information about Ministers and their records. It is very important to note that three
times the then head of Parliamentary Servi ce, Geoff Thorn, said he did not want to
release the information when he was asked, firstly, in two different ways by the Henry
inquiry, and then by Janice Calvert from Mini sterial Services. It was only when the
Prime Minister’s chief of staff, Wayne Eagleson, intervened on 9 May—

So we have Geoff Thorn, we have Davi d Henry, and we have Wayne Eagleson who

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: As I was saying before the dinner break, one of the major
issues within this report is the blurri ng of the lines between the executive and
Parliament. As parliamentarians we guard jealously the privileges and rights that are
given to us here. The distinction between wh at Parliamentary Service does for us as
parliamentarians and what is done for Ministers was one of the issues that arose, but the
significant issue was around the release of data that was about members. As I said
before the break, Geoff Thorn, who was then the head of Parliamentary Service, three
times refused to release that information, but on the intervention of the Prime Minister’s
chief of staff, acting on behalf of the Prime Minister, he did release that information.
We believe, on this side of the House, that  that contradicts what the Prime Minister
said throughout the period of this inquiry—t hat he was not involved in it. He quite
clearly was. He set the terms of reference fo r it. He was the person whose chief of staff
was intimately involved throughout the process and made the very cr itical intervention
that saw data released. As I also noted befo re the dinner break, I am not saying that that
was the only piece of blame that could be appor tioned out of this. It is quite clear there
was plenty of blame to go around, and Davi d Henry and his inquiry team overreached,
but this was the Prime Minister’s inquiry that they were undertaking.
In the time remaining, I want to talk about  a couple of issues. One of those is the
question of metadata versus content, which was a significant debate during the
Government Communications Security Bureau bill. It is worth noting that in this
inquiry, it was the release of metadata—the  so-called information about information—
that was actually critical to what happene d. David Henry found out that there were 86
emails between Peter Dunne and Andrea Vance because of the metadata. Some of that
metadata was not meant to be released, apparently, and that argument—that the
Government felt it was not to be released—is one that I will come to in a minute.
If New Zealanders are to have confiden ce in the security of their information,
metadata is significant. The content of ema ils was requested and eventually some was
released inadvertently, some was released deliberately, and some was pulled back, but it
was that metadata that was the critical elem ent in this investigation. When we are
considering the security of New Zealanders’ data generally, I think we have to bear that
in mind.
This is a sorry saga. The Henry inquiry was poorly run. It wa s poorly set up. Those
involved in it were not conscious of the boundaries between the executive and
Parliament. They rode roughshod over those bo undaries, but at the end of the day New
Zealanders are still none the wi ser as to who actually leak ed the Kitteridge report—a
sensitive, confidential document. The Prime Minister set up an inquiry to do that. Today
he tells us he may let Peter Dunne back into Cabinet, and it is possible for him to do that
only if he believes that someone other than  Peter Dunne leaked the Kitteridge report.
New Zealanders are owed an explanation by  John Key as to who leaked the Kitteridge
report. He has not provided that, and as  a result New Zealanders will not have
confidence in his word.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: Could I just begin my  comments by noting the
remarks of my colleague Kennedy Graham , who sat on the Privileges Committee for
much of the work that led to this interim re port, to the effect that the committee worked
well, was well chaired, and, despite the rather  unfortunate task they were given and the
constraints laid upon them, delivered a useful document. My colleague looks forward to
participating in the work that will lead to a final report next year.
This interim report reflects a bizarre episode in our parliamentary history, an episode
that reflects well on no one who was involved.  The best we can do is to put in place
arrangements to endeavour to ensure there is no repetition of this. The origin of the
whole debacle, of course, li es in the illegal self-empowerment by the Government
4 Dec 2013 Privilege 15255
Communications Security Bureau (GCSB), which came to light more or less by
accident and required the Kitteridge inquiry. That Kitteridge report, as we know now,
was leaked. The Prime Minister then ordered another inquiry to identify the leaker. The
Henry inquiry failed to do that, but did rack up an extraordinar y series of errors that, in
the words of one commentator, would not  be out of place in the script of a Dad’s Army
episode.
The catalyst for the committee’s work was a complaint from our Green co-leader Dr
Russel Norman. The Speaker, in his wisdom, chose not to accept it as a complaint but
referred it instead as a general question of privilege. The result was almost always going
to be unsatisfactory, by definition. The committee was not given the task of finding who
leaked the Kitteridge report, so the public, to a large extent, is none the wiser as to the
facts of the case. What we have  learnt with some clarity is more to do with the dangers
of taking constitutional principles for granted, because this interim report does highlight
some gaps in our practice in that sense. It is when things go wrong that we regret the
lack of clear constitutional guidelines.
We are one of the very few countries in  the world that does not have a written
constitution. It is probably fair to say we  have the least developed mechanisms to
compensate for that lack of a written consti tution. The mistakes of the Henry inquiry
were largely those of indivi duals: excessive zeal, in one case; a relative indifference
from the inquiry leadership to  procedural practice; and an emerging cult that seems to
treat directives from the Prime Minister’s o ffice as some form of holy writ that must be
obeyed. These kinds of problems can be neutralised by constitutional protection.
Without it, they can be exacerbated, and ev en run amok. That is the primary lesson of
the Henry inquiry.
We shed no tears for the ministerial resi gnations throughout this episode, but we do
have considerable sympathy for the Parliame ntary Service resignations, for they were
the product of actions against better j udgment, under duress from the executive.
Diligent and well-intentioned officials ought neve r to be put under that sort of pressure
and should never be subjected to that, and th ere should have been protections in place
against it. The interim report accurately critiques the shortcomings of the whole sorry
affair, and the Green Party endorses this critique. The main test will be the remedial
measures recommended in the final report.
In terms of the process to date, the Green Party is diss atisfied with the decision by
the committee not to have the Prime Minister or the Speaker appear before it. As the
Minister responsible for the GCSB, Mr Key initiated the inquiry, he appointed the co-
commissioners, he was consulte d over the terms of referenc e and the choice of inquiry,
and he publicly released the report. He ac knowledges ministerial responsibility for the
inquiry. He formed the apex of the executiv e branch of Government in this whole
exercise. For his part, the Speaker, being re sponsible for the Parliamentary Service,
formed the apex of the legislative branch in  this matter. He too bears responsibility for
certain aspects of the inquiry. It is difficult to see how the Privileges Committee,
exploring the shortcomings of  an inquiry, could perform th e job entrusted to it, with
some irony, by the Speaker, when the two members of Parliament who bore primary
responsibility for it did not testify.
Then there are the findings of fact. The evid ence gathered in the hearings revealed a
series of avoidable errors—political or pr ocedural—by virtually ev ery individual who
was directly involved in the Key inquir y. Firstly, the Prime Minister decides a
ministerial inquiry should be  set up, appoints the co-commi ssioners, is consulted over
terms of reference and choice of investigat or, receives the report, and makes it public.
He acknowledges he has ministerial responsibil ity, yet his only engagement in his own
inquiry is to declare that he expects all Ministers to cooperate.
15256 Privilege 4 Dec 2013
Secondly, the chief executive officer of th e Department of Prime Minister and
Cabinet is a co-commissioner of the inquiry. The chief executive officer draws up the
terms of consultation with the Prime Minister and is actively engaged in the inquiry, and
yet he is seen as one of the potential suspects. The chief executive officer of the
Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet s econds a staffer to the inquiry. The staffer
acts, we are told, under the supervision of the investigator, yet exercises personal
freedom in visiting Parliamentary Service on his own initiative at a third-tier level,
undermining the authority of the general manager of the Parliamentary Service.
Thirdly, the inquirer adopts a belief that he  is free to ask for any information he
deems necessary without considering whether its release is constitutionally appropriate.
He leaves it to the recipient of the reque st to determine constitutional propriety. He
neither receives nor seeks guidelines on the constitutional and procedural requirements
and constraints pertaining to the operation of a ministerial inquiry. He displays a general
indifference before the committee to the im portance of constitutional constraints. The
main recipient of the request, the Parlia mentary Service, had serious doubts about
releasing information on the communications of  a Minister and journalist, plus their
parliamentary access records, yet it felt co mpelled not to second-guess the request,
because of their security implications. The material does not involve issues of national
security but rather domestic politics, which should have he ightened and not diminished
those concerns.
The chief executive officer of the Prime Minister’s office became engaged. He took
it upon himself to “authorise the Parliamentar y Service to release data pertaining to
Ministers and journalists”. He did this on the basis that the terms of reference had been
made public and that the Prime Minister had ma de it clear that he expected Ministers to
cooperate with the inquiry. Despite three denials by the head of the Parliamentary
Service, nevertheless the Prime Minister’s cock crowed and vowed and the data was
released. In fact, there was no cause for the chief executive officer of the Prime
Minister’s office to become involved in  the inquiry, given that it had been
commissioned by the head of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.
The co-commissioners clearly harboured uncertainty over the particular status of one
Minister who had been given the report in the capacity of coalition party leader, but who
subsequently was expected to cooperate as a Cabinet Minister. This blurred further the
distinction between his role as a member of  the executive, a Government Minister, and
as a member of the legislature, an MP, and it seemed that nobody seemed to care.
No official involved in this whole sorry saga, whether from the Department of the
Prime Minister and Cabinet or the Prime Mini ster’s office, appears to acknowledge that
requests for data pertaining to communica tion between a Minister and a journalist
unavoidably means obtaining information about  a journalist. Refusal to acknowledge
this is strange. They seemed bemused by this self-evident fact through the hearings. The
Evidence Act 2006 protects the rights of a jour nalist to privacy over sources and that is
a well-accepted convention, at least.
The information platform maintained for Ministerial Services and the Parliamentary
Service became operationally merged in late 2011 for reasons, we are told, of
efficiency. This appeared not to bother the Department of the Prime Minister and
Cabinet, the Prime Minister’s office, or th e inquiry. The constitutional separation of
powers appears not to be a ma tter of concern for them either. At no stage did the chief
of the Parliamentary Service discuss matters  of concern with his responsible MP, the
Speaker. At no stage did the Speaker judge it necessary to become engaged in decisions
pertaining to the release of information by the agency un der his control. He should
have.
4 Dec 2013 Privilege 15257
The press gallery has no contractual rela tionship with the Parliamentary Service,
only with the Speaker. A computer technician contracted from a private company took it
upon himself to pass information relating to  a journalist directly to the inquiry.
Although existing legislation pr otects the media from rele asing such information, no
procedural rules were put in place by the inquiry to govern his actions.
The sloppy operation of the inquiry rests on a series of individual misjudgments. The
task remains for the committee in its final report to identify ways in which these
shortcomings can be rectified. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: This is a very sad and sorry
saga. The Prime Minister has acted incompet ently and with a caval ier attitude to his
responsibilities to get at the embarrassing truth, which is that there was a serious leak of
a classified document. I want to say from the outset that if the Prime Minister had
wanted a proper inquiry, he would have, firs t of all, picked someone competent to do
the job; second, provided the powers to do the job properly; and, third, provided the
inquiry with the right terms of reference to  complete the job, which was to find out who
leaked this classified document.
A couple of my colleagues have said that at  the end of the dual sets of inquiries no
one is any the wiser. With respect, yes, I am , because I was the person who said on that
day at the Finance and Expenditure Comm ittee “You leaked the document, didn’t you,
Mr Dunne?”, and that was the beginning of the end. I did not do it because we were
taking a guess or a pot-shot; we knew that he had been the leak—not on one occasion
but on five different occasions. It is not difficult to work out, because you have got four
classified leaks and then you have got one in the Dominion Post, written by the same
journalist, which says that the Inland Re venue Department is helping out in the
Novopay scandal. If you put that all together, you have got to say to yourself “What’s
the common factor here?”. Well, it was th e man who was heading the Inland Revenue
Department. You did not have to be a rocket scientist to work it out. Then there were a
number of what you might call evidentiary matters that we looked at to come to our
conclusion. So at the select committee when that was said to Mr Dunne, we knew where
we were going.
But back to my point—the interim report of the Privileges Committee into the Henry
inquiry following the Kitteridge report leak is a seriously disturbing read on a number
of levels. And anyone who gives a damn  about democracy—and New Zealand First
does—would be deeply unimpressed by what ha s been revealed: something is seriously
rotten in the State of New Zealand.
We have had confirmed what we were sayi ng from the outset that Mr Henry was not
qualified in any way, shape, or form for this  inquiry. What is my evidence? Well, I was
the person who raised, way back in the 1990s, the absolute abomination that was being
foisted upon this country by way of interpre tation of form over substance on the matter
of tax law, and the man heading up the tax department at the time was one David Henry.
He did his utmost to discredit us and trie d to defend these raids on the New Zealand
Treasury and all sorts of illegal activity. Then, just before there was a full-scale—as you
know—commission of inquiry, he jumped ship from the Inland Revenue Department
and set off overseas. So that was our reason for saying that. If he could not get even
such a fundamentally simple thing like the tax law right, why would you repatriate him,
as the Prime Minister did, by giving him a role, first of all, on the Electoral Commission
in this country, then make him a Pike Rive r commissioner, when his forensic ability to
get to the truth is zero, and then make him the inquirer on this matter?
Sure enough—and I am disappointed to say this , as there is nothi ng so antiseptic as
the saying “I told you so.”, but we darn well did. We darn well told all of you that this
man was incompetent. You can laugh and scoff,  but the taxpayer paid him a fortune to
15258 Privilege 4 Dec 2013
do an incompetent job. We had confirmed what  we were saying from the outset: he was
completely inappropriate as an appointment. Of course, that is precisely why Mr Key
picked him for the job. That is why he pi cked him for the job. We have now had an
inquiry but no answers from Mr Henry—just more mud flung in the public space.
He got to the conclusion that it must have  been somewhere near the office of Mr
Peter Dunne, who, by the way, is finding it so difficult to get off his high horse
gracefully. Did you see his press release yesterday? Oh no, he was not going to lose this
massive, long-held, century-ol d right of confidentiality between constituents and an
MP—as though that is what happened. No, no, Mr Dunne, you leaked a classified
document, and in our crimes legislation that is a crime. Just because the police are not
prosecuting you does not mean that you are e xonerated, because they could, and it does
not mean that it is because they are things of no matter. What was being leaked from
that committee was of great importance. The Henry inquiry just left more unanswered
questions, but one of them was not left: who the leaker was. The leaker was a serial
leaker who leaked five times and has been discovered.
It is an indictment on Mr Key and his c ontempt for the democratic process. Our
democracy is not just the right to vote every 3 years. Real democracy is a web of spoken
and unspoken rules and convent ions that give it genuine meaning and not just the
appearance of democracy. To have a proper i nquiry, have the correct terms of reference
so that they can get to the truth, give that person the powers to get to the truth, and then
pick the right person who can be trusted to get to the truth. He did none of those three
things. He just did not care. The privacy of media communications is one of those
aspects that are vital to a f unctioning democracy, and it is a privilege that must not be
abused. The media has a right to be protesti ng in this case, because what happened in
respect of this journalist was constitutio nally and legally just  plain wrong—just plain
wrong.
But Mr Dunne can find no haven in that comp laint, because it does not include him.
The Privileges Committee makes it clear that there was contempt for this principle not
just by Mr Henry but by parliamentary offici als. But, sadly, I think, if the report is
slightly unfair, it is in the fact that these par liamentary officials were being blamed in
circumstances of undue, illegal pressure. In  the end, somebody made a mistake. These
parliamentary officials are the guardians of democratic practices, because if they are
not, who is? But screaming through the inquiry and what came out with our discussions
with these officials was that they had resist ed and resisted and re sisted and in the end
thought: “Well, he has got the powers because the Prime Minister says that he has given
these powers for the investigation, and Minister s must comply.” But, of course, in the
case of Mr Henry, what he did was he di stinguished between Ministers and people on
the select committee, and the leader of the United Future party, as though that was of
any moment whatsoever. It was not, but he distinguished between them. He does it on
page 2 of his report, and he goes straight off track thereafter.
As the Green Party has said, where was the Speaker when all this was happening
right under his nose? Why did he and the Prim e Minister not appear before the select
committee inquiry? The report talks of errors of judgment by parliamentary staff. That
must be understood, I say, within the contex t of undue unlawful pressure. And it leaves
a sour taste, at least in my mouth, that  Mr Thorn has fallen on his sword, has accepted
his accountability, and has gone, and yet the Chief Executive of the Department of the
Prime Minister and Cabinet, Mr Kibblewhi te, offered his resignation but it was not
accepted. How many times have I seen this not  even complicated exercise in deception?
John Key is deeply implicated in this mess, too, but do not expect any accountability
from him.
4 Dec 2013 Privilege 15259
The report of the Privileges Committee is a wake-up call. What this report shows is
how the essential props of democracy can be kicked away. And when John Key is
around, hyper-vigilance is called for. Key and his cronies will trash our democracy like
they are trashing—

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
